children.title: Conic Generator Systems
children.top_down_role: Generation of cones from rays and arbitrary sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be arbitrary. A finite sum over the empty index set is not used; the zero vector is obtained by taking all coefficients equal to zero in a nonempty finite combination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generation is algebraic and uses finite nonnegative combinations. Closure is not inserted into the conic-hull operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conic hull generated by \(S\) is
\[
\operatorname{cone}S:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i s_i:
 r\in\mathbb{N},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}.
\]
A subset \(G\subseteq K\) is a generator system for a convex cone \(K\) when
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}G.
\]
For a finite list \(G=\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}\), this means
\[
K=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j a_j:\mu_j\geq0\right\}.
\]
The system is irredundant when \(a_j\notin\operatorname{cone}(G\setminus\{a_j\})\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic hull of a set consists of all finite nonnegative linear combinations of its elements. A generator system for a cone is a subset whose conic hull equals the cone. A finite generator system gives a matrix-style representation by nonnegative coefficients, and it is irredundant when no listed generator can be generated by the remaining ones.
assumptions_latex: For a generator system, \(K\) is a convex cone and \(G\subseteq K\).
For irredundancy, \(G\) is a finite listed family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}S\) is the set of finite nonnegative combinations of points of \(S\), and \(G\) generates \(K\) exactly when \(K=\operatorname{cone}G\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_r]\), then \(\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}=\{A\mu:\mu\in\mathbb{R}_+^r\}\).
\(\operatorname{cone}S\) is the smallest convex cone containing \(S\).
special_cases_latex: For \(S=\{u\}\) with \(u\neq0\), \(\operatorname{cone}S=\mathbb{R}_+u\) is a ray.
A linear subspace with basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_k\) is generated conically by \(\{\pm b_1,ldots,\pm b_k\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Scaling a generator by a positive scalar does not change its generated ray.
If \(G_1\subseteq G_2\), then \(\operatorname{cone}G_1\subseteq\operatorname{cone}G_2\).
boundary_notes: For infinite \(S\), the algebraic conic hull need not be closed.
Irredundancy of vectors is not the same as uniqueness of nonnegative coefficients.

notation.meaning: Matrix form of a finite conic combination.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Hull Need Not Be Closed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algebraic conic hull can be nonclosed; the displayed set generates the open positive quadrant together with the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=\{(1,t):t>0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), one has \(\operatorname{cone}(S)=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\}\), which is not closed; for example, \((1,1/k)\to(1,0)\notin\operatorname{cone}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This distinguishes the algebraic conic hull from the closed conic hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Hull Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic hull is monotone and idempotent, converts unions into sums, and commutes with linear maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and a linear map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), \(\operatorname{cone}(S\cup T)=\operatorname{cone}(S)+\operatorname{cone}(T)\) and \(A(\operatorname{cone}S)=\operatorname{cone}(A(S))\). Moreover, \(S\subseteq T\) implies \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\subseteq\operatorname{cone}(T)\), and \(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{cone}S)=\operatorname{cone}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(S\cup T)=\operatorname{cone}(S)+\operatorname{cone}(T)\) and \(A(\operatorname{cone}S)=\operatorname{cone}(A(S))\), with monotonicity and idempotence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are algebraic identities; no topological closure is taken.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Carathéodory Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of a conic hull has a conic representation using at most the dimension of the span many linearly independent generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}S)\). Every \(x\in\operatorname{cone}(S)\) can be written as \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i s_i\), where \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), \(r\le d\), and the selected nonzero \(s_i\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i s_i\) for some \(r\le d\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and linearly independent nonzero \(s_i\in S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The sharp bound uses the dimension of the span of S, not necessarily the ambient dimension.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the linear span of S.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic hull of a subset S of Euclidean space consists of all finite nonnegative linear combinations of elements of S, including the empty combination, which equals zero. Thus the conic hull of the empty set is {0}, and the conic hull of S is the smallest convex cone containing S.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its conic hull is
\[
\operatorname{cone}(S):=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i s_i:m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}.
\]
The sum for \(m=0\) is interpreted as \(0\), so \(\operatorname{cone}(\varnothing)=\{0\}\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) is the smallest convex cone containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i s_i:m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq 0\right\}\), where the sum for \(m=0\) equals \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real-vector-space definition, with the convention that the conic hull always contains the origin.

notation.meaning: Conic hull of the set S.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, Section 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Rescaling Invariance of Generator Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent positive rescaling of generators, and insertion or deletion of zero generators, leaves the generated cone unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), choose \(\alpha_s>0\) for every \(s\in S\setminus\{0\}\), and set \(T=\{\alpha_s s:s\in S\setminus\{0\}\}\). Then \(\operatorname{cone}(T)=\operatorname{cone}(S)\). Consequently, if \(S\) generates \(K\), then so does \(T\), and adjoining or deleting zero generators has no effect.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}\{\alpha_s s:s\in S\setminus\{0\}\}=\operatorname{cone}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generators may be rescaled independently; zero vectors may be inserted or removed without changing the generated cone.

notation.meaning: Positive scale assigned to generator s.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Generating Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset S of a convex cone K is a cone generating set when every element of K is a finite nonnegative linear combination of elements of S.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone. A subset \(S\subseteq K\) is a cone generating set for \(K\) precisely when
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}(S).
\]
Thus every \(x\in K\) is a finite nonnegative linear combination of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) generates \(K\) if and only if \(K=\operatorname{cone}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition permits finite or infinite generating sets and does not require generators to be normalized.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, Section 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Generator Systems Need Not Exist
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinitely generated nonclosed cone may have no inclusion-minimal generating system; the open positive quadrant together with the origin is an example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{0\}\cup\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y>0\}\). Then \(K\) is generated, for example, by \(S=\{(1,t):t>0\}\), but it has no inclusion-minimal generating set. Indeed, for any generating set, the slopes of its nonzero elements must have infimum \(0\) and be unbounded above; deleting any one generator preserves those two properties and hence still generates \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no inclusion-minimal set \(S\subseteq K\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying \(\operatorname{cone}(S)=K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The example concerns algebraic generation by arbitrary, possibly infinite sets; it does not contradict existence of irredundant systems for pointed finitely generated cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Generator Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion-minimal finite generating systems for convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a finitely generated convex cone. A finite set \(G\subseteq K\setminus\{0\}\) is a minimal generator system for \(K\) if
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}(G)\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{cone}(G\setminus\{g\})\neq K\ \text{for every }g\in G.
\]
This is inclusion minimality: no generator can be deleted while retaining generation. It does not impose a normalization on generators, so positive rescaling of individual members preserves minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite generator system is minimal when it generates the cone but deleting any one generator destroys that property.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a finitely generated convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is minimal exactly when it generates \(K\) and no proper subset obtained by one deletion generates \(K\).

children.title: Proper Cone Geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Failures of Proper-Cone Conditions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray lacks solidity, a halfspace lacks pointedness, and the open positive quadrant with the origin lacks closedness, showing that the proper-cone hypotheses are independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), \(K_1=\mathbb R_+\times\{0\}\) is closed, convex, and pointed but not solid; \(K_2=\{(x,y):y\ge0\}\) is closed, convex, and solid but not pointed; and \(K_3=\{0\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\}\) is convex, pointed, and solid but not closed. Hence none of solidity, pointedness, or closedness follows from the other two conditions.
assumptions_latex: The proper-cone convention requires convexity, closedness, pointedness, and nonempty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closedness, pointedness, and solidity are nonredundant requirements in the proper-cone definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These examples show why pointedness, solidity, and closedness cannot be dropped from the adopted definition.

notation.meaning: Cones witnessing distinct failures of properness.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper cone in finite-dimensional Euclidean space is a closed convex cone that contains no nontrivial line and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is proper if it is convex and closed, is pointed in the sense that
\[
K\cap(-K)=\{0\},
\]
and is solid in the sense that
\[
\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is proper exactly when it is convex and closed, \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\), and \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the common finite-dimensional convention that a proper cone is closed, convex, pointed, and solid; some sources use different terminology.

children.top_down_role: Finite-generator cone classes and their dimensional organization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finitely generated and polyhedral cone classes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Let \(r,s\) denote positive integers, and let all generator and normal vectors lie in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equivalence of finite generation and polyhedrality is finite-dimensional. The class includes cones with lineality and cones of dimension smaller than the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the finitely generated cone class and the polyhedral cone class by
\[
\mathcal{FG}_n:=\left\{\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}:r<\infty\right\},
\]
\[
\mathcal{PC}_n:=\left\{\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:b_j^Tx\leq0, j=1,\ldots,s\}:s<\infty\right\}.
\]
The finite-dimensional Minkowski–Weyl correspondence identifies these classes:
\[
\mathcal{FG}_n=\mathcal{PC}_n.
\]
A cone in either class is therefore called finitely generated or polyhedral. If it admits linearly independent generators \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) with \(k=\dim K\), it is simplicial in its span.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely generated cone is the conic hull of finitely many vectors. A polyhedral cone is the intersection of finitely many homogeneous closed halfspaces. In finite-dimensional spaces these are exactly the same class. A cone is simplicial in its span when it can be generated by as many linearly independent vectors as its dimension.
assumptions_latex: The generator list and homogeneous inequality list are finite.
For the simplicial designation, the chosen generators are linearly independent and their number equals \(\dim K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is finitely generated if and only if it is polyhedral, i.e. \(\mathcal{FG}_n=\mathcal{PC}_n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\in\mathcal{FG}_n\iff K=A\mathbb{R}_+^r\) for some finite matrix \(A\).
\(K\in\mathcal{PC}_n\iff K=\{x:Bx\leq0\}\) for some finite matrix \(B\).
special_cases_latex: Every ray and every finitely generated linear subspace belongs to \(\mathcal{FG}_n\).
The nonnegative orthant is both simplicial and polyhedral.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finitely generated cone in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed.
Every polyhedral cone possesses a finite generator system.
boundary_notes: The equality of the two classes is a finite-dimensional result.
A finite generator list need not be irredundant or unique.

notation.meaning: Class of finitely generated cones in R^n.
Class of polyhedral cones in R^n.

source_refs.locator: §2.3.1, definitions of polyhedral and finitely generated cones, and Proposition 2.3.2, “Minkowski-Weyl Theorem”

knowledge_statements.title: Duals of Finitely Generated Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a finitely generated cone is cut out by one inequality per displayed generator and is itself finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), then \(K^*=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,v_i\rangle\ge0, i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Hence \(K^*\) is polyhedral and therefore finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,v_i\rangle\ge0\ \forall i\}\) is finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The positive-dual convention \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\) is used.

knowledge_statements.title: Faces Inherit Finite Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face of a finitely generated cone is generated by precisely those displayed generators that lie in the face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) and \(F\) is a face of \(K\), then \(F=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:v_i\in F\}\). In particular, every face of a finitely generated cone is finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:v_i\in F\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formula applies to every face, including the zero face and the whole cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure of the Finite-Generation Class under Conic Operations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear images, finite sums, finite intersections, and finite products of finitely generated cones are again finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finite-dimensional finitely generated cones are closed under linear images, finite Minkowski sums, finite intersections, and finite Cartesian products. Thus, if \(K_1,\ldots,K_p\) are finitely generated and \(A\) is linear, then \(A(K_1)\), \(K_1+\cdots+K_p\), \(K_1\cap\cdots\cap K_p\), and \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_p\) are finitely generated cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K_1,\ldots,K_p\) are finitely generated cones in finite-dimensional spaces.
\(A\) is a linear map with finite-dimensional codomain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(K_1)\), \(\sum_iK_i\), \(\bigcap_iK_i\), and \(\prod_iK_i\) are finitely generated cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All spaces and indexed families are finite-dimensional and finite, respectively.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski–Weyl Theorem for Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional convex cone is finitely generated exactly when it is the solution set of finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the following are equivalent: \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) for some finite family, and \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}\) for some finite matrix \(A\). Thus finitely generated cones are exactly polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is finitely generated if and only if \(K\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the homogeneous finite-dimensional Minkowski–Weyl equivalence.

notation.meaning: Matrix whose rows define homogeneous linear inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Finitely Generated Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex cones generated by finitely many vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone. The cone \(K\) is finitely generated if there exist \(m\in\mathbb{N}_0\) and vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\in E\) such that
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}(\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\})=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\geq0\right\}.
\]
In finite-dimensional real vector spaces, finitely generated cones are exactly polyhedral cones, meaning intersections of finitely many closed homogeneous halfspaces. In particular, every finitely generated cone is convex and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional real vector space, a cone is finitely generated when finitely many vectors generate it by nonnegative combinations; these cones are exactly the polyhedral cones.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is finitely generated exactly when \(K=\operatorname{cone}(\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\})\) for some finite family; equivalently, \(K\) is polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Dual of a Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside its span, the dual of a simplicial cone is generated by the dual basis and is again simplicial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}K\) and \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\) be simplicial. If \(w_1,\ldots,w_d\in L\) is the dual basis, \(\langle w_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\), then \(K_L^*:=\{y\in L:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}=\operatorname{cone}\{w_1,\ldots,w_d\}\). Thus the relative dual is simplicial.
assumptions_latex: \(w_1,\ldots,w_d\) is dual to the simplicial generator basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_L^*=\operatorname{cone}\{w_1,\ldots,w_d\}\) is simplicial.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a non-full-dimensional cone, the ambient dual additionally contains \((\operatorname{span}K)^\perp\); simpliciality here concerns the dual inside the span.

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Face Lattice of a Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a simplicial cone is generated by a subset of its rays, so its face lattice is Boolean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\) be simplicial. Its faces are exactly \(F_I=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:i\in I\}\), where \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Moreover, \(\dim F_I=|I|\), and inclusion, intersection, and generated join correspond respectively to subset inclusion, intersection, and union of index sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F(K)=\{F_I:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\}\) and \(\dim F_I=|I|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The empty subset corresponds to the zero face and the full subset to K.

notation.meaning: Face generated by the rays indexed by I.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthant Representation and Unique Coordinates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A d-dimensional simplicial cone is linearly isomorphic to the nonnegative orthant and every point has unique nonnegative coordinates in its ray generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\) with \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\) linearly independent, then \(T:\mathbb R^d\to\operatorname{span}K\), \(T(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i v_i\), is an isomorphism satisfying \(T(\mathbb R_+^d)=K\). Consequently every \(x\in K\) has a unique representation \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i v_i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\mathbb R_+^d)=K\), and every \(x\in K\) has unique nonnegative coordinates in \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The isomorphism is between the cone's span and \(\mathbb R^d\), so it covers cones not full-dimensional in the ambient space.

notation.meaning: Coordinate isomorphism from the orthant to K.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplicial Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cones generated by linearly independent rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone, and set \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\). The cone \(K\) is simplicial if there exist linearly independent nonzero vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\in E\) such that
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}(\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}).
\]
Equivalently, \(K\), considered within \(\operatorname{span}K\), is linearly isomorphic to the nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb{R}_+^d\). The coefficients in the representation of each element of \(K\) relative to \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\) are unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplicial cone of dimension d is generated by d linearly independent rays, is linearly equivalent within its span to the nonnegative orthant, and has unique coefficients relative to those generators.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone with \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is simplicial exactly when it has \(d\) linearly independent generators.

notation.meaning: dimension of the linear span of K

source_refs.locator: §19. Polyhedral Convex Sets and Functions p. 170

source_witnesses.locator: §19. Polyhedral Convex Sets and Functions p. 170

knowledge_statements.title: Dependent Displayed Generators Do Not Imply Nonsimpliciality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone can have a dependent finite presentation while remaining simplicial; redundant generators must first be removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2\}=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,e_2\}=\mathbb R_+^2\). The displayed three-generator family is linearly dependent and redundant, but \(K\) is simplicial.
assumptions_latex: \(e_1,e_2\) are the standard basis of \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2\}\) is simplicial despite its dependent displayed generating family.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsimpliciality concerns the existence of an independent generating system, not whether a particular presentation is dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Extreme-Ray Coordinates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed nonsimplicial finitely generated cone has more extreme rays than its dimension and some nonzero point has two different decompositions using extreme-ray generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be pointed and finitely generated, let \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\), and choose nonzero representatives \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) of its distinct extreme rays. If \(K\) is nonsimplicial, then \(r>d\), and there exist distinct \(\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R_+^r\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i v_i=\sum_{i=1}^r\mu_i v_i\ne0\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is pointed, finitely generated, and nonsimplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r>d\) and \(\exists\lambda\ne\mu\in\mathbb R_+^r\) with \(\sum_i\lambda_i v_i=\sum_i\mu_i v_i\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The claim concerns representatives of all distinct extreme rays of a pointed nonsimplicial cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsimplicial Finite Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-ray criterion for pointed finitely generated cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a pointed finitely generated cone, and set \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\). Then \(K\) has finitely many extreme rays and
\[
K\text{ is simplicial}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\text{ has exactly }d\text{ extreme rays}.
\]
Consequently, \(K\) is nonsimplicial if and only if it has more than \(d\) extreme rays. In that case, any family consisting of exactly one nonzero representative from each extreme ray is linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed finitely generated d-dimensional cone is nonsimplicial exactly when it has more than d extreme rays; one representative from each extreme ray then forms a linearly dependent family.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a pointed finitely generated cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is nonsimplicial if and only if the number of its extreme rays exceeds \(d\).

notation.meaning: dimension of the linear span of K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces, exposed faces, and extreme rays of a cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone containing \(0\). Let \(K^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces and extreme rays are defined for arbitrary convex cones. The generation consequence is stated only for nontrivial closed pointed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex subset \(F\subseteq K\) is a face of \(K\) when
\[
x,y\in K,\ 0<\lambda<1,\ \lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in F
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x,y\in F.
\]
It is exposed when there exists \(y\in K^\circ\) such that
\[
F=K\cap y^\perp=\{x\in K:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}.
\]
For \(u\in K\setminus\{0\}\), the ray \(\mathbb{R}_+u\) is an extreme ray exactly when it is a one-dimensional face; equivalently,
\[
x_1,x_2\in K,\ x_1+x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+u
\Rightarrow x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+u.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face of a convex cone is a convex subset that contains both endpoints whenever it contains an interior point of a segment in the cone. An exposed face is obtained by intersecting the cone with a supporting hyperplane through the origin. Extreme rays are precisely the one-dimensional faces and are characterized by indecomposability: a vector on the ray cannot be written as a sum of cone vectors outside the ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Faces, exposed faces, and extreme rays are characterized by the displayed segment, supporting-hyperplane, and decomposition conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mathbb{R}_+u\) is extreme iff it is a half-line face emanating from the origin.
For a cone, a nonempty exposed face has the form \(K\cap y^\perp\) for a polar vector \(y\).
special_cases_latex: The faces \(\{0\}\) and \(K\) are called improper faces when they satisfy the face condition.
If \(K\) is closed, pointed, and nonzero, vectors chosen from all extreme rays generate \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed ray is an extreme ray.
A face of a face of \(K\) is a face of \(K\).
boundary_notes: Not every face of a general closed convex cone is exposed.
A cone with nonzero lineality has no extreme rays in directions affected by that lineality; facial analysis is commonly reduced modulo the lineality space.

notation.meaning: Optional notation indicating that F is a face of K.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence Boundary for Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero closed finite-dimensional convex cone has an extreme ray exactly when it is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\ne\{0\}\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space. Then \[K\text{ has an extreme ray}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\text{ is pointed}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\ne\{0\}\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) possesses an extreme ray if and only if \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional existence criterion for nonzero closed convex cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional faces of a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone and let \(r\in K\setminus\{0\}\). The ray \(R=\{\lambda r:\lambda\geq0\}\) is an extreme ray of \(K\) if, whenever \(x,y\in K\) and \(x+y\in R\), one has \(x,y\in R\). Equivalently, \(R\) is a one-dimensional face of \(K\). The definition depends only on the ray, since replacing \(r\) by any positive multiple leaves \(R\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray is extreme when a sum of two cone elements can lie on it only if both summands lie on that same ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is extreme exactly when \(x+y\in R\) with \(x,y\in K\) implies \(x,y\in R\).

notation.meaning: ray generated by the nonzero vector r

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Is Contained in Every Nonempty Conic Face
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face is a cone containing the original cone's lineality space; the origin is a face exactly for pointed cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(K\). Then \(F\) is a convex cone and \[\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\subseteq F.\] Consequently, \(\{0\}\) is a face of \(K\) if and only if \(K\) is pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a convex cone, \(\operatorname{lin}K\subseteq F\), and \(\{0\}\unlhd K\iff K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural constraint on the facial hierarchy of a convex cone.

notation.meaning: F is a face of K.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection and Transitivity of Conic Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of a cone are closed under intersections, and a face of a face is a face of the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every intersection of nonempty faces of a convex cone \(K\) is a face of \(K\). Moreover, if \(G\) is a face of \(F\) and \(F\) is a face of \(K\), then \(G\) is a face of \(K\).
assumptions_latex: Faces use the ordinary segment criterion, equivalently the additive conic criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_i\unlhd K\Rightarrow\bigcap_iF_i\unlhd K\), and \(G\unlhd F\unlhd K\Rightarrow G\unlhd K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary closure properties of the facial hierarchy of a convex cone.

notation.meaning: F is a face of K.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces specialized to convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone. A convex cone \(F\subseteq K\) is a face of \(K\) if
\[
x,y\in K,
\quad x+y\in F
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x,y\in F.
\]
Equivalently, viewed as a convex subset, \(F\) has the segment-face property: if a point of the relative interior of a segment \([x,y]\subseteq K\) lies in \(F\), then both endpoints lie in \(F\). The sets \(\{0\}\) and \(K\) are faces whenever \(K\) is pointed for the former.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic face absorbs both cone summands whenever their sum belongs to it; this agrees with the usual segment definition of a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a face of \(K\) exactly when \(x+y\in F\) and \(x,y\in K\) imply \(x,y\in F\).

notation.meaning: closed line segment joining x and y

knowledge_statements.title: Ray-Face Incidence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme rays of a face F are exactly the extreme rays of the ambient cone K that lie in F.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a face of a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(R\subseteq F\) be a nonzero ray. Then
\[
R\text{ is an extreme ray of }F
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
R\text{ is an extreme ray of }K.
\]
Consequently, the extreme rays incident with \(F\) are exactly the extreme rays of \(K\) that are contained in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is an extreme ray of \(F\) if and only if \(R\) is an extreme ray of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This incidence statement applies only to rays contained in the specified face.

notation.meaning: Nonzero ray contained in the face.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, with the standard inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\). The polar convention uses nonpositive pairings.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polarity is defined for an arbitrary nonempty set. Its value is always a closed convex cone, independently of whether the original set is closed, convex, or conic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar cone and positive dual cone of \(C\) are
\[
C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\forall x\in C)\;\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\},
\qquad C^*:=-C^\circ
 =\{y:(\forall x\in C)\;\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\}.
\]
Polarity is order reversing:
\[
C\subseteq D\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D^\circ\subseteq C^\circ.
\]
It ignores closure, convexification, and conic generation:
\[
C^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}C)^\circ=(\operatorname{conv}C)^\circ=(\operatorname{cone}C)^\circ.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone contains the vectors pairing nonpositively with every point of the original set. The positive dual cone is its negative and uses nonnegative pairings. Polarity reverses inclusions and depends only on the closed convex cone generated by the original set. The polar is always a closed convex cone.
assumptions_latex: The Euclidean inner product fixes the polarity convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in C\}\), \(C^*=-C^\circ\), and polarity is antitone and invariant under closure, convex hull, and conic hull.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(C=\operatorname{cone}S\), then \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,s\rangle\leq0\ \forall s\in S\}\).
For a subspace \(L\), \(L^\circ=L^\perp\).
special_cases_latex: \((\mathbb{R}_+^n)^\circ=\mathbb{R}_-^n\) and \((\mathbb{R}_+^n)^*=\mathbb{R}_+^n\).
\(\{0\}^\circ=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \((\mathbb{R}^n)^\circ=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(C^\circ\) is a closed convex cone.
For cones \(K_1,K_2\), \((K_1+K_2)^\circ=K_1^\circ\cap K_2^\circ\).
boundary_notes: Some sources use the symbol \(C^*\) for the nonpositive polar; the sign convention must therefore be checked.
The polar cannot distinguish a set from its closed convex conic hull.

notation.meaning: Positive dual cone, equal to the negative polar.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Calculus for Conic Sums and Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity converts conic sums into intersections and intersections into closures of sums of polar cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K,L\) be closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional inner-product space. Then \[(K+L)^\circ=K^\circ\cap L^\circ,\qquad (K\cap L)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}(K^\circ+L^\circ).\] The closure in the second identity may be omitted when \(K^\circ+L^\circ\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(K,L\) are closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((K+L)^\circ=K^\circ\cap L^\circ\) and \((K\cap L)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}(K^\circ+L^\circ)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic algebraic rules for negative polar cones, including the necessary closure boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Depends Only on the Closed Convex Conic Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking a polar retains only the closed convex cone generated by the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every subset \(C\) of a real Hilbert space, \[C^\circ=(\operatorname{cone}C)^\circ=(\overline{\operatorname{cone}C})^\circ,\] where \(\operatorname{cone}C\) denotes the convex conic hull. Thus a generating set and the closed convex cone it generates impose exactly the same polar inequalities.
assumptions_latex: The polar uses the nonpositive-pairing convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=(\overline{\operatorname{cone}C})^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical invariance and generator representation of a polar cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Cone Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone of C consists of all vectors having nonpositive inner product with every element of C. It is a closed convex cone, and polarity reverses set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq H\). The polar cone of \(C\) is
\[
C^{\circ}:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in C\}
=\bigcap_{x\in C}\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\}.
\]
It is always a closed convex cone, and \(C\subseteq D\) implies \(D^{\circ}\subseteq C^{\circ}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ}=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }x\in C\}\), and \(C^{\circ}\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the polar-cone convention with nonpositive inner products; the dual cone under the nonnegative convention is \(-C^{\circ}\).

notation.meaning: Polar cone of C under the nonpositive-pairing convention.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, Section 6.3, Polar and Dual Cones, p. 122

children.top_down_role: Recovery and closure under repeated cone polarity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar completion of a set or cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, and use the nonpositive polar \(C^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The general formula applies to an arbitrary nonempty set. Its specializations distinguish arbitrary cones, convex cones, and closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bipolar completion operator is
\[
\mathcal{B}(C):=C^{\circ\circ}=(C^\circ)^\circ.
\]
The cone bipolar theorem gives
\[
C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}C).
\]
Equivalently, if \(K\) is already a cone,
\[
K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}K).
\]
Consequently, for a convex cone \(K\),
\[
K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K,
\]
and for a closed convex cone, \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar is obtained by applying the polar operation twice. For any nonempty set it equals the closed convex cone generated by that set. If the original object is a cone, the bipolar is its closed convex hull; if it is already convex, the bipolar merely closes it; and if it is closed and convex, polarity twice recovers it exactly.
assumptions_latex: The same inner product and nonpositive-polar convention are used in both polar operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}C)\), with the stated cone, convex-cone, and closed-convex-cone specializations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}\) is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(C\).
\(x\in C^{\circ\circ}\iff\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\) satisfying \(\langle y,c\rangle\leq0\) for all \(c\in C\).
special_cases_latex: For a subspace \(L\), \(L^{\circ\circ}=L\).
For a ray \(K=\mathbb{R}_+u\), \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The bipolar operator is extensive, monotone, and idempotent.
Two nonempty sets have the same polar exactly when their closed convex conic hulls coincide.
boundary_notes: Exact recovery of the original set fails unless it is a closed convex cone.
The formula concerns conic polarity and differs from polar-set constructions normalized by an inequality such as \(\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\).

source_refs.locator: §2.2, Proposition 2.2.1(b), “Polar Cone Theorem,” and the paragraph immediately following it

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex-Cone Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex cone in a real Hilbert space, taking the polar cone twice recovers the original cone exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, and let \(K\subseteq H\) be a closed convex cone. Define
\[
K^{\circ}:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.
\]
Then the bipolar recovers the cone exactly:
\[
K^{\circ\circ}=K.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq H\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone bipolar theorem in a real Hilbert space, specialized to exact recovery of a closed convex cone.

notation.meaning: Polar cone under the nonpositive-pairing convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact recovery as a bipolar fixed point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty cone, and define \(K^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record isolates the exact-recovery regime from the more general bipolar closure formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed convex-cone recovery class is the fixed-point family
\[
\operatorname{Fix}(\circ\circ):=\{K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:K\neq\varnothing,\ K^{\circ\circ}=K\}.
\]
It is exactly the family of nonempty closed convex cones:
\[
K^{\circ\circ}=K
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
K\text{ is a closed convex cone}.
\]
Equivalently, every closed convex cone admits the exact halfspace representation
\[
K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\forall y\in K^\circ)\;\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is recovered exactly from all of its polar inequalities precisely when it is closed and convex. Thus the fixed points of the double-polar operation are exactly the nonempty closed convex cones. In that regime, membership in the cone is equivalent to satisfying every homogeneous linear inequality indexed by its polar cone.
assumptions_latex: Polarity is taken with respect to the Euclidean inner product and the nonpositive convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\) if and only if \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in K\iff\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in K^\circ\).
Closed convex cones are exactly the fixed points of the closure operator \(C\mapsto C^{\circ\circ}\).
special_cases_latex: Every closed linear subspace satisfies \(L^{\circ\circ}=L\).
Every polyhedral cone is recovered exactly because it is closed and convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: A closed convex cone is completely determined by its polar cone.
If two closed convex cones have identical polars, then the cones are equal.
boundary_notes: Closedness and convexity are both essential for exact recovery.
The result recovers the cone as a set; it does not select a finite inequality representation.

notation.meaning: Fixed-point family of the bipolar operator.

children.title: Nonclosed-Cone Closure Regime
children.top_down_role: Closure effects for cones lacking topological completeness.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Inequalities Cannot Detect Missing Boundary Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a convex cone does not change its dual, so dual inequalities cannot detect points omitted only from the cone's boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Then \[K^*=(\operatorname{cl}K)^*.\] Hence, if \(x\in\operatorname{cl}K\setminus K\), then \(\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in K^*\); no positive-dual inequality strictly separates \(x\) from \(K\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=(\operatorname{cl}K)^*\), and missing boundary points admit no strictly negative positive-dual separator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information lost when bipolarity replaces a nonclosed convex cone by its closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Cone Closure Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar of a finite-dimensional convex cone is its closure. Hence a nonclosed cone is strictly smaller than its bipolar, while a closed convex cone equals its bipolar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every convex cone \(K\) in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, its bipolar equals its closure:
\[K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K.\]
Thus a nonclosed convex cone is recovered from its bipolar only after closure.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone, not necessarily closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K.\] Consequently, \(K^{**}=K\) holds if and only if \(K\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone bipolar theorem using the positive-dual convention; the closure is essential when the cone is not closed.

notation.meaning: Dual cone with the nonnegative-pairing convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar closure of a nonclosed convex cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex cone that is not assumed closed, and use the nonpositive polar convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the convex but potentially nonclosed specialization of the bipolar theorem. Nonconvex cones require convexification as well as closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bipolar closure completion of \(K\) is
\[
\widehat K:=K^{\circ\circ}.
\]
For every nonempty convex cone,
\[
\widehat K=K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K.
\]
Hence, in the genuinely nonclosed regime,
\[
K\subsetneq K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K.
\]
Polarity is insensitive to the missing boundary:
\[
K^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}K)^\circ,
\]
so polar data recover the closure rather than the original nonclosed cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex cone that is not assumed closed, taking the polar twice produces exactly its topological closure. If the cone is genuinely nonclosed, the original cone is strictly contained in its bipolar. The cone and its closure have the same polar, so no reconstruction based only on polar inequalities can distinguish which boundary points were originally omitted.
assumptions_latex: For the strict inclusion, \(K\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K\), and if \(K\) is nonclosed then \(K\subsetneq K^{\circ\circ}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{cl}K\iff\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in K^\circ\).
\(K^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}K)^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is already closed, the completion is exact: \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
For an arbitrary nonconvex cone \(Q\), \(Q^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}Q)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: All cones lying between \(K\) and \(\operatorname{cl}K\) and having the same closure possess the same polar.
The bipolar completion is idempotent: \(\widehat K^{\circ\circ}=\widehat K\).
boundary_notes: Double polarity cannot recover deliberately deleted boundary points.
For a nonconvex cone, closure alone is insufficient; convexification also occurs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-dual cones under a fixed inner product
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality depends on the selected inner product. The definition uses the positive dual cone, not the nonpositive polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The positive dual cone and nonpositive polar are
\[
K^*:=\{y\in E:(\forall x\in K)\;\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\},
\qquad K^\circ=-K^*.
\]
The self-dual regime is
\[
\mathfrak{SD}(E):=\{K\subseteq E:K\text{ is a nonempty convex cone and }K=K^*\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
K\in\mathfrak{SD}(E)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K^\circ=-K.
\]
Because every dual cone is closed and convex, a self-dual cone is automatically a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive dual cone consists of vectors pairing nonnegatively with every cone vector. A cone is self-dual when it equals this positive dual under the chosen inner product. Equivalently, its nonpositive polar is its negative. Self-duality automatically supplies closedness and convexity, but it is not invariant under arbitrary changes of inner product.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone.
The same fixed inner product defines both the dual and self-duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is self-dual iff \(K=K^*\), equivalently iff \(K^\circ=-K\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in K\iff\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\).
Using nonpositive polarity, self-duality is the relation \(K=-K^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: The nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is self-dual under the standard Euclidean inner product.
The cone of positive semidefinite symmetric matrices is self-dual under the Frobenius inner product.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every self-dual cone is closed and convex.
In a nonzero finite-dimensional ambient space, a self-dual cone is pointed and full-dimensional.
boundary_notes: Changing the inner product can change the dual cone and hence self-duality.
With the nonpositive-polar convention, writing \(K=K^\circ\) is not the standard self-duality relation.

notation.meaning: Family of self-dual cones in E.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Cones Are Proper
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nonzero finite-dimensional inner-product space, every self-dual cone is closed, pointed, and full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\ne\{0\}\) be finite-dimensional and let \(K\subseteq E\) satisfy \(K=K^*\). Then \(K\) is closed, pointed, and full-dimensional: \[K\cap(-K)=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{span}K=E,\qquad \operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing.\] Thus \(K\) is a proper cone.
assumptions_latex: \(E\ne\{0\}\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone satisfying \(K=K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is closed, pointed, and full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural consequences of equality with the dual cone.

notation.meaning: Positive dual cone under the specified inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Cone Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is self-dual for a specified inner product when it equals the cone of all vectors having nonnegative inner product with every vector in the cone. Such a cone is necessarily closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex cone \(K\) is self-dual with respect to \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) when
\[K=K^*,\qquad K^*:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\]
This equality implies that \(K\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality is defined relative to the displayed inner product and the positive-dual convention.

notation.meaning: Dual cone induced by the specified inner product.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, §6.3, “Polar and Dual Cones,” p. 122

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Cones Are Necessarily Non-Self-Dual
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed cone cannot equal its closed dual, although closedness alone does not imply self-duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every cone \(K\) in a finite-dimensional inner-product space, \(K^*\) is closed. Therefore \[K\text{ nonclosed}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad K\ne K^*.\] The converse fails: a closed cone may still be non-self-dual.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
Duality uses the fixed nonnegative-pairing convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonclosedness implies \(K\ne K^*\), but the converse is false.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness obstruction to self-duality under a fixed inner product.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the fixed inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Self-Dual Cone Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is non-self-dual for a specified inner product when it differs from its dual cone. For example, the nonnegative horizontal ray in the plane has the right half-plane as its Euclidean dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex cone \(K\) is non-self-dual with respect to \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) when
\[K\ne K^*,\qquad K^*:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\]
For example, under the Euclidean inner product on \(\mathbb R^2\), the ray \(K=\{(t,0):t\ge0\}\) has dual \(K^*=\{(u,v):u\ge0\}\), so \(K\ne K^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record defines failure of self-duality for a fixed inner product; the same cone may behave differently under another inner product.

notation.meaning: Dual cone induced by the specified inner product.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, §6.3, “Polar and Dual Cones,” p. 122

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Change as a Euclidean Coordinate Transformation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring the metric converts a change of inner product into an invertible coordinate transformation; metric self-duality becomes Euclidean self-duality of the transformed cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=T^{\mathsf T}T\), where \(G\) is symmetric positive definite and \(T\) is invertible. Then \(T:(\mathbb R^n,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_G)\to(\mathbb R^n,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is an isometry and \[(TK)^*=T^{-\mathsf T}K^*.\] Consequently, \[K=K^{*_{G}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad TK=(TK)^*.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((TK)^*=T^{-\mathsf T}K^*\) and \(K=K^{*_{G}}\iff TK=(TK)^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isometric coordinate form of pairing-dependent cone duality.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the G-inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality Dependence on Inner Products
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an inner product is represented by a symmetric positive-definite matrix G, then the corresponding dual cone is the inverse image of the Euclidean dual under G. Thus self-duality can change when the inner product changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K^*\) denote the Euclidean dual cone and let \(K^{*_{G}}\) denote the dual under \(\langle x,y\rangle_G=x^{\mathsf T}Gy\). Then
\[K^{*_{G}}=\{y:y^{\mathsf T}Gx\ge0\text{ for every }x\in K\}=G^{-1}K^*.\]
Consequently,
\[K=K^{*_{G}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad GK=K^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(E=\mathbb R^n\) carries the Euclidean inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^{\mathsf T}y\).
\(G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K^{*_{G}}=G^{-1}K^*.\] In particular, \(K\) is self-dual under \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_G\) if and only if \(GK=K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coordinate representation of how changing the inner product changes the dual cone.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the Euclidean inner product.
Dual cone under the inner product induced by the positive-definite matrix.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, §6.3, “Polar and Dual Cones,” p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-based sufficient criteria for closed images and sums
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are finite-dimensional sufficient criteria. They control escaping sequences through recession directions lying in a map kernel or canceling across a Minkowski sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the linear-image asymptotic closedness condition by
\[
\mathrm{AC}_{\mathrm{im}}(A,C):
\quad \operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C.
\]
Whenever this condition holds,
\[
AC:=\{Ax:x\in C\}\text{ is closed}.
\]
For nonempty closed convex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_r\), define the sum condition
\[
\mathrm{AC}_{\mathrm{sum}}(C_1,\ldots,C_r):
\quad d_i\in\operatorname{rec}C_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^r d_i=0
\Rightarrow d_i\in\operatorname{lin}C_i\ \forall i.
\]
Whenever it holds,
\[
C_1+\cdots+C_r\text{ is closed}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set satisfies the linear-image asymptotic closedness condition when every recession direction annihilated by the linear map is reversible lineality. This condition guarantees that the image is closed. For a Minkowski sum, the corresponding condition requires every collection of recession directions that cancels to zero to consist entirely of lineality directions; this guarantees that the sum is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) and every \(C_i\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
For the sum criterion, each \(d_i\) belongs to \(\operatorname{rec}C_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C\Rightarrow AC\) is closed, and the displayed zero-sum recession condition implies that \(C_1+\cdots+C_r\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A stronger image condition is \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\).
For two sets, the sum condition is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rec}C_1\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C_2)\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C_1\cap(-\operatorname{lin}C_2)\).
special_cases_latex: The linear image of every polyhedral set is closed.
If one summand is compact, its recession cone is \(\{0\}\), eliminating cancellation through that summand.
immediate_consequences_latex: A closed convex set with no nonzero kernel recession direction has a closed linear image.
The criterion applies to projections by taking \(A\) to be a coordinate projection.
boundary_notes: The image condition is sufficient and is not asserted to be necessary in full generality.
Without recession regularity, a linear image or Minkowski sum of closed convex sets can fail to be closed.

children.title: Nested Closed-Set Intersection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Intersection behavior controlled by boundedness and recession structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Selection Criterion for Nested Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested sequence of nonempty closed sets has nonempty intersection exactly when one can select a bounded point from every level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((C_k)_{k\geq1}\) be a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space. Then
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k\neq\varnothing
\]
if and only if there exists a bounded sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq1}\) satisfying \(x_k\in C_k\) for every \(k\).
assumptions_latex: The ambient normed space is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_kC_k\neq\varnothing\) if and only if there is a bounded sequence with \(x_k\in C_k\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential certificate for nonemptiness of a decreasing closed-set intersection in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: one selected point from each nested set

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Closed Sets May Escape to Infinity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing sequence of nonempty closed convex sets can escape to infinity and have empty intersection when no member is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C_k=[k,+\infty)\subset\mathbb R\), every \(C_k\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(C_{k+1}\subset C_k\). Nevertheless,
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k=\varnothing.
\]
Each member is unbounded and satisfies \(\operatorname{rec}(C_k)=[0,+\infty)\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{k+1}\subset C_k\) for every \(k\), but \(\bigcap_{k\geq1}C_k=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of nested-intersection nonemptiness when no member is bounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Cantor Singleton Intersection Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested nonempty closed sets with one bounded member and diameters tending to zero have a singleton intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((C_k)_{k\ge1}\) be a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space. If some \(C_m\) is bounded and
\[
\operatorname{diam}(C_k)\longrightarrow0,
\]
then there exists a unique point \(x_*\) such that
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k=\{x_*\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \((C_k)_{k\ge1}\) is decreasing and every \(C_k\) is nonempty and closed.
The ambient normed space is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{k\ge1}C_k\) consists of exactly one point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singleton refinement for nested closed sets whose diameters vanish.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Recession Criterion for Nested Convex Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If nested nonempty closed convex sets have empty intersection, they share a nonzero recession direction; hence trivial common recession guarantees intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((C_k)_{k\geq1}\) be a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space. Then
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k=\varnothing
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{rec}(C_k)\text{ contains a nonzero vector}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{rec}(C_k)=\{0\}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}C_k\neq\varnothing.
\]
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_k\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The ambient normed space is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Empty intersection implies a common nonzero recession direction; therefore \(\bigcap_k\operatorname{rec}(C_k)=\{0\}\) implies \(\bigcap_k C_k\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-geometric condition preventing a decreasing sequence of closed convex sets from escaping to infinity.

notation.meaning: recession cone of the kth closed convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Closed-Set Intersection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nested-intersection criterion using common recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1\supseteq C_2\supseteq\cdots\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\). If
\[
\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{rec}(C_n)=\{0\},
\]
then \(\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}C_n\ne\varnothing\). In particular, this conclusion holds if some \(C_n\) is bounded; in that case the intersection is compact. Equivalently, if the nested intersection is empty, the sets possess a common nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested nonempty closed convex sets intersect when they have no common nonzero recession direction; a bounded member guarantees this and makes the intersection compact.
assumptions_latex: \(C_n\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_n\operatorname{rec}(C_n)=\{0\}\) implies \(\bigcap_n C_n\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\{C_k\}_{k\geq 0}\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(C_{k+1}\subseteq C_k\). Write \(R_k=\operatorname{rec}(C_k)\), \(L_k=R_k\cap(-R_k)\), \(R=\bigcap_{k\geq0}R_k\), and \(L=\bigcap_{k\geq0}L_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nested sequences are classified by compactness, common recession geometry, and retractiveness. These are sufficient-regime definitions, not an assertion that every nonempty intersection satisfies one of them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence is in the compact regime if some \(C_j\) is bounded. It is in the lineality-balanced regime if \(R=L\). An asymptotic sequence is a sequence \(x_k\in C_k\setminus\{0\}\) for which \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) and \(x_k/\|x_k\|\to d/\|d\|\) for some \(d\in R\setminus\{0\}\). Such a sequence is retractive if \(x_k-d\in C_k\) for all sufficiently large \(k\); the nested family is retractive when every asymptotic sequence is retractive. These conditions define the principal nested closed-set intersection regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing sequence of nonempty closed convex sets is in the compact regime when one member is bounded, and in the lineality-balanced regime when its common recession cone equals its common lineality space. An unbounded selection is asymptotic when its normalized vectors converge to a nonzero common recession direction. It is retractive when subtraction of that direction eventually leaves every selected vector in its corresponding set; the family is retractive if this holds for every asymptotic selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{compact regime: }\exists j\ C_j\text{ bounded};\qquad \text{balanced regime: }R=L;\qquad \text{retractive regime: }\forall\{x_k\}\text{ asymptotic},\ \exists k_0\ \forall k\geq k_0,\ x_k-d\in C_k.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), boundedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{0\}\).
The equality \(R=L\) says that every common recession direction is reversible in every \(C_k\).
special_cases_latex: If some \(C_j\) is compact, then every later \(C_k\) lies in the compact set \(C_j\).
A constant sequence \(C_k=C\) is retractive exactly when the closed convex set \(C\) is retractive in the corresponding single-set sense.
immediate_consequences_latex: A retractive nested sequence has nonempty intersection.
If \(R=L\), then the intersection is nonempty and has the form \(L+K\) for some nonempty compact convex set \(K\).
boundary_notes: Nestedness and closedness are essential to the stated regime terminology.
Retractiveness is sufficient for nonemptiness but is not necessary.
The definition is finite-dimensional; compactness and subsequence arguments require modification in general topological vector spaces.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of a nonempty closed convex set.
Lineality space of the kth set.
Common recession cone and common lineality space.

children.title: Closedness Under Linear Maps
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic criteria for preservation of closedness under linear transformation.

knowledge_statements.title: Trivial Recession Kernel Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The seed's recession-kernel test is sufficient but not necessary: the zero map sends the whole line to a closed singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closedness of \(A(C)\) does not imply \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\). For \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and the zero map \(A:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\), \(A(C)=\{0\}\) is closed, while \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(C)\text{ closed}\centernot\Longrightarrow \operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of the seed criterion, not an example of a nonclosed image.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Relaxed Recession Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image is closed when the recession directions annihilated by the map form only reversible lineality; requiring that intersection to be zero is a stronger special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, with \(E,F\) finite-dimensional. If \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\) is a linear subspace, then \(A(C)\) is closed. The seed condition \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) is the zero-subspace special case.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(C)\text{ is closed in }F.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A broader finite-dimensional sufficient condition than the seed's trivial-intersection criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Trivial Recession Kernel as Properness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absence of a nonzero kernel recession direction is equivalent to properness of the restricted map and therefore guarantees a closed image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, where \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear. Then \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) if and only if \(C\cap A^{-1}(K)\) is compact for every compact \(K\subseteq F\). Equivalently, \(A|_C:C\to F\) is proper; consequently \(A(C)\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\iff \forall K\subseteq F\text{ compact},\ C\cap A^{-1}(K)\text{ is compact};\quad A(C)\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent compact-preimage formulation of the seed's stronger sufficient condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Under Linear Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient recession-kernel criterion for closed linear images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. If
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C)\cap\ker A=\{0\},
\]
then the image \(A(C):=\{Ax:x\in C\}\) is a closed convex subset of \(\mathbb R^m\). The condition rules out unbounded sequences in \(C\) that escape along directions annihilated by \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image of a closed convex set is closed when the set has no nonzero recession direction lying in the map's kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(C)\) is closed and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-regular closedness under a linear map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. Put \(R_C=\operatorname{rec}(C)\), \(L_C=R_C\cap(-R_C)\), and \(N(A)=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition isolates a standard finite-dimensional sufficient regime for preservation of closedness. It does not claim that the recession condition is necessary whenever the image happens to be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((C,A)\) is recession-regular for closed images if \(R_C\cap N(A)\subseteq L_C\). It is strongly recession-regular if \(R_C\cap N(A)=\{0\}\). The set \(C\) is closed-image stable under \(A\) when \(A(C)\) is closed, equivalently when every convergent sequence \(Ax_j\to y\) with \(x_j\in C\) has a point \(x\in C\) satisfying \(Ax=y\). Recession regularity is the asymptotic criterion defining the canonical guaranteed-closedness regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set and a linear map form a recession-regular pair when every recession direction annihilated by the map is a lineality direction of the set. Strong regularity requires the only annihilated recession direction to be zero. Closed-image stability means that the linear image is closed, or equivalently that every limit of image points has a preimage in the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_C\cap\ker A\subseteq L_C\ \Longrightarrow\ A(C)\text{ is closed}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(A(C)\text{ is closed}\iff \forall (x_j)\subset C,\ Ax_j\to y\Rightarrow \exists x\in C:\ Ax=y.\)
The condition \(R_C\cap\ker A\subseteq L_C\) means that no irreversible escape direction of \(C\) is collapsed to zero by \(A\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, then \(R_C=\{0\}\), so \(A(C)\) is compact and closed.
If \(A\) is injective, then \(\ker A=\{0\}\), so strong recession regularity holds.
The image of a polyhedral convex set under any linear map is polyhedral and hence closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under recession regularity, \(\operatorname{rec}(A(C))=A(R_C)\).
The stronger condition \(R_C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) is an immediately checkable sufficient criterion.
boundary_notes: A continuous linear image of an arbitrary closed set need not be closed.
For nonclosed or nonconvex domains, the recession criterion in this form does not apply.
Failure of recession regularity signals possible degeneracy but does not by itself force nonclosedness.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the domain set.
Lineality space of the domain set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is compact in a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(A\) is linear, then \(A(C)\) is compact and hence closed. In particular, every nonempty compact convex set satisfies \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp logical boundary of the seed criterion; this is not a nonclosed-image pathology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closedness of \(A(C)\) does not imply \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\). For example, with \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and the zero map \(A:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\), one has \(A(C)=\{0\}\), which is closed, but \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession-kernel test is sufficient but not necessary: the zero map sends the whole line to a closed singleton despite annihilating every recession direction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthens and equivalently formulates the immutable seed's sufficient closed-image condition in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, where \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear. Then \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) if and only if \(C\cap A^{-1}(K)\) is compact for every compact \(K\subseteq F\). Equivalently, the restriction \(A|_C:C\to F\) is proper. Under these conditions, \(A(C)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absence of a nonzero recession direction in the kernel is equivalent to properness of the map restricted to the closed convex set, and therefore guarantees a closed image.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\iff \forall K\subseteq F\text{ compact},\ C\cap A^{-1}(K)\text{ is compact};\quad A(C)\text{ is closed}.

children.title: Nonclosed Linear-Image Regimes
children.top_down_role: Closedness failures produced by asymptotic degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Witnesses of Nonclosed Linear Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing image limit can only be approached through unbounded preimages, whose normalized escape directions yield nonzero recession directions annihilated by the map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, where \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. If \(x_k\in C\), \(Ax_k\to z\), and \(z\notin A(C)\), then \((x_k)\) is unbounded. For any \(c\in C\), every convergent subsequence of \((x_k-c)/\|x_k-c\|\) has a unit limit \(d\in C^\infty\cap\ker A\). Conversely, nonclosedness of \(A(C)\) supplies such a sequence for some \(z\in\overline{A(C)}\setminus A(C)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Missing image limits have unbounded preimage witnesses with unit cluster directions in \(C^\infty\cap\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary escape behavior of preimages approaching a missing image point.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Linear-Image Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite-cone projection exhibiting loss of closedness under a linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\mathbb S_+^2\), the closed convex cone of real positive-semidefinite matrices \(X=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\), and define the linear map \(A(X)=(a,b)\). Then
\[
A(C)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},
\]
which is not closed: \((1/n,1)\in A(C)\) for every positive integer \(n\), while \((1/n,1)\to(0,1)\notin A(C)\). Hence a linear image of a closed convex cone need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting the two-by-two positive-semidefinite cone onto its first diagonal and off-diagonal entries produces a convex but nonclosed image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(C)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\) is not closed.

notation.meaning: cone of real two-by-two positive-semidefinite symmetric matrices
