knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Distance Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is tangent exactly when a step of length t in that direction misses the set by an amount negligible relative to t.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real normed vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in C\). For every \(d\in X\),
\[
d\in T_C(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x+td,C)}{t}=0.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed vector space.
\(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\in T_C(x)\iff\lim_{t\downarrow0}t^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(x+td,C)=0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This metric formulation characterizes the closed tangent cone of a closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Tangent Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed tangent cone at x is the norm closure of the radial cone. Equivalently, its directions are limits of rescaled displacements from x to nearby points of C.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real normed vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be convex, and let \(x\in C\). The closed tangent cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is \[T_C(x):=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}=\overline{R_C(x)}.\] Equivalently, \[T_C(x)=\left\{d\in X:\exists\,t_n\downarrow0,\ \exists\,x_n\in C,\ \frac{x_n-x}{t_n}\to d\right\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_C(x):=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}=\overline{R_C(x)}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the norm-closed convex tangent cone, also called the Bouligand tangent cone in this convex setting.

notation.meaning: closed tangent cone of C at x
radial cone of C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the structural universal property of the closed tangent cone for a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real normed vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be convex, and let \(x\in C\). Then \(T_C(x)\) is a closed convex cone and is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(C-x\). Equivalently, for every closed convex cone \(K\subset X\),
\[
C-x\subseteq K\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_C(x)\subseteq K.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed tangent cone is the smallest closed convex cone containing all displacements from the base point to the set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_C(x)\text{ is the smallest closed convex cone containing }C-x.

children.title: Tangent Location Regimes
children.top_down_role: Variation of tangent geometry with facial location.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(L:=\operatorname{lin}(C-C)\), and let \(x\in C\). Tangent cones are understood relative to the affine hull through the subspace \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets; the classification separates full-dimensional interior, relative interior, and relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The tangent location regime of \(x\) is determined by its membership in \(\operatorname{int}C\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\), or \(\operatorname{rbd}C\). Precisely, \[x\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff T_C(x)=L.\] Consequently, if \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(L=\mathbb R^n\) and \(T_C(x)=\mathbb R^n\). If \(x\in\operatorname{rbd}C\), then \(T_C(x)\subsetneq L\) is a proper closed convex cone and has a nonzero supporting normal relative to \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every relative-interior point, the tangent cone is the full subspace parallel to the affine hull. At an ordinary interior point this is the whole ambient space. At a relative-boundary point the tangent cone is a proper cone inside the affine-hull direction space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff T_C(x)=L,\qquad x\in\operatorname{rbd}C\iff T_C(x)\subsetneq L.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff N_C(x)=L^\perp.\]
For full-dimensional \(C\), \[x\in\operatorname{int}C\iff N_C(x)=\{0\}\iff T_C(x)=\mathbb R^n.\]
special_cases_latex: For a polyhedron, the relative-boundary regime is determined by its active inequalities.
For a singleton, \(L=\{0\}\), its unique point lies in the relative interior, and its tangent cone is \(\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Only relative-boundary points yield a proper tangent approximation within \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
The normal cone enlarges as the point moves from relative interior to lower-dimensional facial locations.
boundary_notes: Ordinary interior is empty for lower-dimensional convex sets, so relative interior is the intrinsic notion.
A boundary point of a full-dimensional set may still have a tangent cone containing a nontrivial lineality space.

notation.meaning: linear subspace parallel to the affine hull of C

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Tangent Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an ambient interior point of a convex set, every direction is locally feasible, so both the radial and closed tangent cones equal the entire space; in a Hilbert space the normal cone is trivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real normed vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\). Then every \(d\in X\) is feasible for a sufficiently small positive step, and therefore \[R_C(x)=T_C(x)=X.\] If \(X\) is a real Hilbert space, this is equivalent to \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior is taken in the ambient norm topology, not relative to the affine hull.

notation.meaning: radial and closed tangent cones at x

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Point Tangent Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a boundary point of a closed convex set with nonempty interior, there is a nonzero supporting normal. Every tangent direction lies in the corresponding closed halfspace, so the tangent cone is not the whole space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{int}C\neq\varnothing\), and let \(x\in\partial C\). Then there exists \(u\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\), and \[T_C(x)\subset\{d\in H:\langle u,d\rangle\leq0\}.\] Hence \(T_C(x)\neq H\); the tangent cone is constrained by at least one supporting normal direction.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{int}C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists\,u\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\quad\text{such that}\quad T_C(x)\subset\{d\in H:\langle u,d\rangle\leq0\}\neq H.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The nonempty ambient-interior assumption ensures the supporting-normal boundary characterization stated here.

notation.meaning: normal cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Tangent Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a relative-interior point of a lower-dimensional convex set, the tangent cone is the direction space parallel to the affine hull, and the normal cone is its orthogonal complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and set \(L=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\). If \(\dim L<n\), then \[T_C(x)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}=L\quad\text{and}\quad N_C(x)=L^\perp.\] Thus the tangent cone is a proper linear subspace rather than the whole ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(x)=L\) and \(N_C(x)=L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the relative-interior regime for a convex set whose affine hull has dimension strictly below the ambient Euclidean space.

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone, defined as the closure of the conic hull of the feasible displacements

children.title: Normal Cone Family
children.top_down_role: Supporting directions and local dual geometry at a point.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. The Euclidean inner product identifies linear functionals with vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-analytic normal cones; this is not a nonconvex limiting-normal construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in C\), the normal cone is \[N_C(x):=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:\langle s,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C\}.\] The normal-cone family is the set-valued mapping \(N_C:C\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), \(x\mapsto N_C(x)\). Equivalently, \(s\in N_C(x)\) when the linear functional \(y\mapsto\langle s,y\rangle\) attains its maximum over \(C\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal-cone family assigns to each point all vectors defining supporting half-spaces of the convex set at that point. A vector is normal precisely when its linear functional is maximized at the base point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_C(x)=\{s:\langle s,y\rangle\le\langle s,x\rangle\ \forall y\in C\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[s\in N_C(x)\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle.\]
\[s\in N_C(x)\iff x=P_C(x+s).\]
\[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\).
For \(C=\{y:\langle a,y\rangle\le b\}\) and \(\langle a,x\rangle=b\), \(N_C(x)=\mathbb R_+a\).
For a polyhedron, the normal cone is generated by the normals of active inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Each \(N_C(x)\) is a closed convex cone containing \(0\).
boundary_notes: At points outside \(C\), this record does not define a normal cone.
For nonconvex sets, proximal, regular, and limiting normal cones are generally different.

children.title: Supporting Normals
children.top_down_role: Normal directions arising from local support.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximizer and Orientation Tests for Supporting Normals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero vector supports the set at x exactly when x maximizes its linear functional. Positive multiples preserve support, while the opposite orientation also supports precisely when the entire set lies in the contact hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(x\in C\), and let \(v\neq0\). Then \(v\) is a supporting normal to \(C\) at \(x\) if and only if \[x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle v,y\rangle,\] equivalently \(\sigma_C(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\). If \(v\) is supporting, then every \(\lambda v\), \(\lambda>0\), is supporting at \(x\). Moreover, both \(v\) and \(-v\) are supporting at \(x\) if and only if \(C\subset H(v,x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ supports }C\text{ at }x\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle v,y\rangle\iff\sigma_C(v)=\langle v,x\rangle, with positive-ray invariance and the stated criterion for reversal.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive rescaling preserves the oriented supporting halfspace. Reversing the normal generally does not; both orientations support at the same point exactly when the whole set lies in the contact hyperplane.

notation.meaning: support function of C evaluated at v
hyperplane through x with normal v

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting Normals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting normal at a point is a nonzero vector perpendicular to a hyperplane through that point such that the entire convex set lies in the corresponding closed halfspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(x\in C\), a supporting normal to \(C\) at \(x\) is a vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\] Equivalently, \(C\) lies in the closed halfspace \(\{y:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\}\), and \(H(v,x)=\{y:\langle v,y-x\rangle=0\}\) is a supporting hyperplane of \(C\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A supporting normal at \(x\) is a vector \(v\neq0\) satisfying \(\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The zero vector belongs to every normal cone but is excluded from the term supporting normal because it does not determine a hyperplane.

notation.meaning: supporting hyperplane with normal v through x

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.4 and 7.1, Tangent and Normal Cones and Support Points, pp. 125 and 133

children.title: Facial Normal-Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Dependence of local dual geometry on the containing face.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal cone as the cone of exposing directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For \(s\in\mathbb R^n\), define the exposed face \(F_C(s):=\{y\in C:\langle s,y\rangle=\sigma_C(s)\}\), where \(\sigma_C(s):=\sup_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional facial geometry; empty exposed faces are allowed when the support supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial normal-cone geometry at \(x\in C\) is the incidence correspondence \[N_C(x)=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:x\in F_C(s)\}=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle=\sigma_C(s)\}.\] Hence the normal cone consists exactly of directions exposing faces that contain \(x\). If \(F\) is a face of \(C\) and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), its facial normal cone is well defined by \[N_C(F):=N_C(x),\] because this value is constant on \(\operatorname{ri}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal geometry and facial geometry are linked by incidence: a vector is normal at a point exactly when that point belongs to the face exposed by the vector. The normal cone is constant over the relative interior of a fixed face, so it can be attached to the face itself.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s\in N_C(x)\iff x\in F_C(s)\iff \langle s,x\rangle=\sigma_C(s).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[N_C(x)=\{s:x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle\}.\]
special_cases_latex: At a relative-interior point of \(C\), \(N_C(x)=\operatorname{lin}(C-C)^\perp\).
For a polyhedron, points with the same active face have the same cone generated by active constraint normals.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F\subseteq G\) are faces and both relative interiors are nonempty, then \(N_C(G)\subseteq N_C(F)\).
A nonzero element of \(N_C(x)\) identifies a supporting hyperplane through \(x\).
boundary_notes: Different faces may share the same normal cone when the facial structure is not exposed sufficiently to distinguish them.
The whole set is the face exposed by \(s=0\).

notation.meaning: face of C exposed by direction s
normal cone at any relative-interior point of F

knowledge_statements.title: Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cone at a point consists of all vectors making a nonpositive inner product with every feasible displacement from that point. It is a closed convex cone, and its nonzero vectors are supporting normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(x\in C\), its normal cone at \(x\) is \[N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.\] It is a closed convex cone, and its nonzero elements are precisely the supporting normals to \(C\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}\), a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the convex-analytic normal cone with the outward-normal sign convention.

notation.meaning: normal cone of C at x

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.4, Tangent and Normal Cones, p. 125

children.title: Normal Geometry on Relative Interiors of Faces

knowledge_statements.title: Normal Geometry on Relative Interiors of Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the relative interior of the same face has the same normal cone. A vector belongs to this cone exactly when its linear functional is maximized over the convex set at every point of the face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a nonempty face of a convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). For any \(x,z\in\operatorname{ri}F\), \[N_C(x)=N_C(z)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:F\subseteq\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle v,y\rangle\}.\] Hence the normal cone is constant on \(\operatorname{ri}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)=N_C(z)=\{v:F\subseteq\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle v,y\rangle\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constancy holds on the relative interior of any nonempty face; the maximizer set may strictly contain the face when the face is not exposed.

notation.meaning: relative interior of the face F

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.4 and 7.1, Tangent and Normal Cones and Support Points, pp. 125 and 133

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Face Inclusion Need Not Strictly Enlarge Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The endpoint of a flat boundary ray can be a proper subface while having the same downward normal ray as the relative interior of the larger face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(s)=(\max\{s,0\})^2,\qquad C=\operatorname{epi}f\subset\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
and set
\[
F=\{(0,0)\},\qquad G=\{(s,0):s\leq0\}.
\]
Then \(F\subsetneq G\) are faces of \(C\), \((0,0)\in\operatorname{ri}F\), and \((s,0)\in\operatorname{ri}G\) for every \(s<0\), but
\[
N_C(0,0)=N_C(s,0)=\{(0,-\lambda):\lambda\geq0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\subsetneq G\quad\text{but}\quad N_C(0,0)=N_C(s,0)=\{(0,-\lambda):\lambda\geq0\}\quad(s<0).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outside the polyhedral regime, a proper facial inclusion can preserve the normal cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Normal-Cone Growth for Polyhedral Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For polyhedra, descending properly to a smaller face strictly enlarges the normal cone; its dimension is the ambient dimension minus the face dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, and let \(F\subsetneq G\) be nonempty faces of \(C\). If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\) and \(z\in\operatorname{ri}G\), then
\[
N_C(z)\subsetneq N_C(x).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\dim N_C(x)=n-\dim F,\qquad \dim N_C(z)=n-\dim G.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_C(z)\subsetneq N_C(x),\qquad \dim N_C(x)=n-\dim F,\quad \dim N_C(z)=n-\dim G.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral facial incidence strengthens the general inclusion to strict inclusion for proper face containment.

notation.meaning: dimension of the affine hull of face F

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Growth Across Face Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Face inclusion reverses normal-cone inclusion: a boundary face contained in a larger face has at least all the normal directions of the larger face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq G\) be nonempty faces of a convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\) and \(z\in\operatorname{ri}G\), then \[N_C(z)\subseteq N_C(x).\] Thus moving from the relative interior of a larger face into a boundary face can only enlarge the normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(G\) are nonempty faces of \(C\) with \(F\subseteq G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(z)\subseteq N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inclusion need not be strict without additional hypotheses, especially for non-exposed faces.

notation.meaning: normal cone of C at a relative-interior point of a face

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.4 and 7.1, Tangent and Normal Cones and Support Points, pp. 125 and 133

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face Inclusion Need Not Strictly Enlarge Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A proper facial inclusion can preserve the normal cone in nonpolyhedral geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(s)=\max\{0,s^2\},\qquad C=\operatorname{epi}f\subset\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
and define
\[
F=\{(0,0)\},\qquad G=\{(s,0):s\leq0\}.
\]
Then \(F\subsetneq G\) are faces of \(C\), \((0,0)\in\operatorname{ri}F\), and every \((s,0)\) with \(s<0\) lies in \(\operatorname{ri}G\), but
\[
N_C(0,0)=N_C(s,0)=\{(0,-\lambda):\lambda\geq0\}.
\]
Thus the order-reversing normal-cone inclusion associated with \(F\subsetneq G\) need not be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The endpoint of a flat boundary ray can be a proper subface while having the same downward normal ray as the relative interior of the larger face. Proper face inclusion therefore need not cause strict normal-cone growth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\subsetneq G\quad\text{but}\quad N_C(0,0)=N_C(s,0)=\{(0,-\lambda):\lambda\geq0\}\ \text{for every }s<0.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Inclusion Need Not Strictly Enlarge Normal Cones

children.title: Normal Smoothness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Single-normal and multi-normal boundary geometries.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a full-dimensional closed convex set and let \(x\in C\). The normal cone \(N_C(x)\) contains all outward supporting directions at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-dimensional finite-dimensional convex sets; smoothness here is defined only through uniqueness of the supporting normal ray, not differentiability of a parametrized boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A boundary point \(x\in\partial C\) is in the single-normal regime when there exists a nonzero vector \(n_x\), unique up to positive scaling, such that \[N_C(x)=\mathbb R_+n_x.\] It is in the multi-normal regime when \(N_C(x)\) contains two non-collinear nonzero vectors, equivalently \(\dim N_C(x)\ge2\). Interior points form the zero-normal regime, characterized by \[N_C(x)=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary point is single-normal when all supporting normals lie on one ray. It is multi-normal when at least two non-collinear supporting normals occur. Interior points have only the zero normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed, convex, and full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\begin{cases}N_C(x)=\{0\},&x\in\operatorname{int}C,\\N_C(x)=\mathbb R_+n_x,&x\in\partial C\ \text{in the single-normal regime},\\\dim N_C(x)\ge2,&x\in\partial C\ \text{in the multi-normal regime}.\end{cases}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The single-normal condition is equivalent to uniqueness, up to positive scaling, of the nonzero linear functional maximized over \(C\) at \(x\).
The multi-normal condition is equivalent to the existence of distinct supporting hyperplanes through \(x\) with nonparallel normals.
special_cases_latex: A boundary point of a closed half-space is single-normal.
A vertex of a full-dimensional polyhedron is typically multi-normal; its normal cone is generated by the active facet normals.
immediate_consequences_latex: In the single-normal regime, \(T_C(x)=\{d:\langle n_x,d\rangle\le0\}\).
In the multi-normal regime, \(T_C(x)\) is the intersection of at least two nonredundant supporting homogeneous half-spaces.
boundary_notes: For lower-dimensional \(C\), every normal cone contains \(\operatorname{lin}(C-C)^\perp\); an intrinsic smoothness convention should quotient out that subspace.
Uniqueness of a normal ray does not by itself assert second-order smoothness or curvature.

notation.meaning: representative nonzero outward normal at x
nonnegative ray generated by the normal

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Normal Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-dimensional convex set is in the smooth normal regime at a boundary point when the normal cone is a single ray, equivalently when there is a unique supporting hyperplane there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed, convex, and full-dimensional, and let \(x\in\partial C\). The boundary is in the smooth normal regime at \(x\) when there exists \(v\neq0\) such that \[N_C(x)=\mathbb{R}_+v.\] Equivalently, \(C\) has exactly one supporting hyperplane at \(x\), up to positive rescaling of its outward normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary is in the smooth normal regime at \(x\) exactly when \(N_C(x)=\mathbb{R}_+v\) for some \(v\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness here means uniqueness of the supporting-normal direction, not differentiability of a boundary parametrization.

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.4 and 7.1, Tangent and Normal Cones and Support Points, pp. 125 and 133

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Normal Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary point is in the nonsmooth normal regime when its normal cone has more than one ray, equivalently when the point admits distinct supporting hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed, convex, and full-dimensional, and let \(x\in\partial C\). The boundary is in the nonsmooth normal regime at \(x\) when \(N_C(x)\) is not a ray. Equivalently, there exist non-collinear vectors \(v_1,v_2\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\), so at least two distinct supporting hyperplanes pass through \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary is in the nonsmooth normal regime at \(x\) exactly when \(N_C(x)\) is not a ray, equivalently when it contains two non-collinear nonzero vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The full-dimensional assumption removes normal directions caused solely by embedding a lower-dimensional set in a larger ambient space.

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.4 and 7.1, Tangent and Normal Cones and Support Points, pp. 125 and 133

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Inner Semicontinuity at a Multiplicity Transition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the quadrant's vertex the normal cone gains horizontal negative components that cannot be approximated while approaching along one edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\mathbb{R}_+^2\), \(x=(0,0)\), and \(x_k=(1/k,0)\). Then \(x_k\to x\), while
\[
N_C(x)=\mathbb{R}_-^2,
\qquad
N_C(x_k)=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}_-.
\]
Consequently \((-1,-1)\in N_C(x)\), but no sequence \(v_k\in N_C(x_k)\) converges to \((-1,-1)\). Thus the normal-cone mapping can fail to be inner semicontinuous where normal multiplicity increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (-1,-1)\in N_C(x)\quad\text{but no }v_k\in N_C(x_k)\text{ satisfies }v_k\to(-1,-1).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-graph outer stability does not make every limiting-point normal approximable along an arbitrary convergent sequence of nearby points.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal Multiplicity Transition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limits of normals at converging points remain normal at the limit point. Normal multiplicity means that the unit-normal section at the limiting point contains more than one direction; this does not imply that every such direction occurs at a distinct nearby smooth point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), the normal-cone mapping has closed graph: if \(x_k\to x\), \(v_k\to v\), and \(v_k\in N_C(x_k)\) for every \(k\), then \(v\in N_C(x)\). At a point with multiple unit normal directions, the set \(N_C(x)\cap\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\) contains more than one element. Thus every convergent selection of nearby normals has a limit that remains normal at the limiting point, without asserting that all normal directions are realized at distinct nearby smooth points.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k\to x\), \(v_k\to v\), and \(v_k\in N_C(x_k)\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in N_C(x)\); at a point \(x\) with multiple unit normal directions, \(N_C(x)\cap\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\) contains more than one element.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This records the closed-graph constraint on convergent selections of normals and identifies multiplicity through the unit-normal section. It does not assert realization of every limiting normal by normals at distinct nearby smooth points.

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.4, Tangent and Normal Cones, p. 125

children.title: Tangent-Normal Polarity
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence between feasible local directions and supporting normals.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mutual polarity of tangent and normal cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x\in C\), and use the negative polar \(K^\circ:=\{s:\langle s,d\rangle\le0\ \forall d\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets with closed tangent cones and the negative-polar sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Tangent-normal polarity at \(x\) is the mutual-polar relation \[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,\qquad T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.\] Equivalently, a vector \(s\) is normal at \(x\) precisely when it pairs nonpositively with every tangent direction, and a vector \(d\) is tangent precisely when it pairs nonpositively with every normal: \[s\in N_C(x)\iff \langle s,d\rangle\le0\ \forall d\in T_C(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent and normal cones at a point are exact polar duals. Normals are precisely the vectors nonpositive on every tangent direction, and tangent directions are precisely the vectors nonpositive on every normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bigl(T_C(x),N_C(x)\bigr)=\bigl(N_C(x)^\circ,T_C(x)^\circ\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in T_C(x)\iff \sup_{s\in N_C(x)}\langle s,d\rangle\le0.\]
\[s\in N_C(x)\iff \sup_{y\in C}\langle s,y-x\rangle\le0.\]
special_cases_latex: At an interior point, the polar pair is \((\mathbb R^n,\{0\})\).
At the vertex of a closed convex cone \(K\), the pair is \((K,K^\circ)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Inclusion reverses under polarity: enlargement of the tangent cone corresponds to contraction of the normal cone.
Each cone determines the other uniquely.
boundary_notes: Using the positive dual cone changes the sign in the pairing.
For nonconvex sets, regular and limiting tangent-normal constructions need not be mutual polars.

notation.meaning: negative polar of a cone K

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Is Unnecessary for Convex Local Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set, the closed tangent cone and convex-analytic normal cone are mutually polar even when the set itself is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(x\in C\), and define \[T_C(x)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)},\qquad N_C(x)=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}.\] With \(K^\circ=\{v:\langle v,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\), one has \[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\quad\text{and}\quad T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\) and \(T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This sharpens the seed's assumptions when the tangent cone is defined as the closed conic hull of C-x; the set C itself need not be closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Polar Pairing
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At any point of a closed convex set, the normal cone is the negative polar of the tangent cone, and the tangent cone is the negative polar of the normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(x\in C\), define \(K^\circ=\{v:\langle v,k\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }k\in K\}\). Then the local tangent and normal cones form a polar pair: \[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\quad\text{and}\quad T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\) and \(T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The polar convention uses nonpositive inner products; under a nonnegative dual-cone convention a minus sign is required.

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.3–6.4, Polar and Dual Cones and Tangent and Normal Cones, pp. 122–125

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, let \(x\in C\), and let \(T:=T_C(x)\) and \(N:=N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local primal-dual geometry at one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local polar pairing is the restriction of the Euclidean bilinear form to \(N\times T\): \[\pi_x:N\times T\to\mathbb R_-,\qquad \pi_x(s,d):=\langle s,d\rangle.\] Its defining order property is \(\pi_x(s,d)\le0\) for all \((s,d)\in N\times T\), together with the recovery formulas \[N=\{s:\pi_x(s,d)\le0\ \forall d\in T\},\qquad T=\{d:\pi_x(s,d)\le0\ \forall s\in N\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local polar pairing evaluates a normal against a tangent direction. It is always nonpositive, and either local cone can be recovered as the set of all vectors pairing nonpositively with the other cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\pi_x(s,d)=\langle s,d\rangle\le0\quad\forall(s,d)\in N_C(x)\times T_C(x),\] with each cone equal to the polar determined by this pairing.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For subsets \(D\subseteq T\) and \(S\subseteq N\), define \[D^{\triangle}:=\{s\in N:\langle s,d\rangle=0\ \forall d\in D\},\quad S^{\triangle}:=\{d\in T:\langle s,d\rangle=0\ \forall s\in S\}.\] These are the zero-pair sets induced by \(\pi_x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(N=\{0\}\), the pairing is identically zero and \(T=\mathbb R^n\).
For \(C=K\) and \(x=0\), the pairing is the usual polar pairing between \(K^\circ\) and \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The zero level \(\langle s,d\rangle=0\) selects complementary tangent and normal directions.
The pairing is invariant under positive rescaling of either cone element.
boundary_notes: Nonpositive pairing is the polar condition; equality is the stronger complementarity condition.
The codomain \(\mathbb R_-\) follows from the negative-polar convention.

notation.meaning: zero-pair operator within the local tangent-normal pair

children.title: Tangent-Normal Complementarity
children.top_down_role: Orthogonal relationships between active directions and normals.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, \(x\in C\), \(d\in T_C(x)\), and \(s\in N_C(x)\). Polarity always gives \(\langle s,d\rangle\le0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional first-order complementarity at a fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tangent-normal pair \((d,s)\) is complementary at \(x\) when \[d\in T_C(x),\qquad s\in N_C(x),\qquad \langle s,d\rangle=0.\] For fixed \(s\), the complementary tangent directions form the exposed cone face \[F_T(s):=T_C(x)\cap s^\perp.\] For fixed \(d\), the complementary normals form \[F_N(d):=N_C(x)\cap d^\perp.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangent direction and a normal are complementary when their polar inequality is active, meaning that they are orthogonal. Fixing either member selects the orthogonal exposed face of the opposite cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(d,s)\ \text{is complementary at }x\iff \langle s,d\rangle=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in F_T(s)\iff s\in F_N(d).\]
\[F_T(s)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in T_C(x)}\langle s,v\rangle,\] where the maximum equals \(0\).
special_cases_latex: For cone projection, \(d=P_K(z)\) and \(s=P_{K^\circ}(z)\) form a complementary pair.
For a polyhedron, complementary tangent directions keep every constraint with a positive normal multiplier active to first order.
immediate_consequences_latex: Both \(F_T(s)\) and \(F_N(d)\) are closed convex cone faces.
Positive rescaling of \(d\) or \(s\) preserves complementarity.
boundary_notes: Membership in the polar cones alone yields only a nonpositive inner product; orthogonality must be imposed separately.
This definition is local and does not assert global optimality of an optimization problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Tangent-Normal Orthogonality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every normal is orthogonal to every reversible tangent direction, meaning a direction for which both signs are tangent. General tangent-normal pairs need only have nonpositive inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(x\in C\), and let \(n\in N_C(x)\). If \(d\in\operatorname{lin}T_C(x)=T_C(x)\cap(-T_C(x))\), then \[\langle n,d\rangle=0.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle n,d\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary tangent and normal directions satisfy only a nonpositive inner-product inequality; equality is guaranteed for tangent directions in the lineality space.

notation.meaning: lineality space of the tangent cone

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.3–6.4, Polar and Dual Cones and Tangent and Normal Cones, pp. 122–125

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Complementarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vector decomposes uniquely into an orthogonal tangent component and normal component obtained by projecting onto the local tangent and normal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x\in C\), and let \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Since \(T_C(x)\) and \(N_C(x)\) are mutually polar closed convex cones, \[z=P_{T_C(x)}z+P_{N_C(x)}z,\qquad \left\langle P_{T_C(x)}z,P_{N_C(x)}z\right\rangle=0.\] The two summands are uniquely determined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=P_{T_C(x)}z+P_{N_C(x)}z\) and \(\langle P_{T_C(x)}z,P_{N_C(x)}z\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is Moreau decomposition applied to the mutually polar local tangent and normal cones.

notation.meaning: Euclidean metric projection onto the closed convex cone K

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 4.3, 6.3, and 6.4, Projectors onto Convex Sets, Polar and Dual Cones, and Tangent and Normal Cones, pp. 74 and 122–125

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Face Complementarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron, tangent directions satisfy the linearized active inequalities and normals are nonnegative combinations of active constraint normals. A tangent-normal pair is orthogonal exactly when every positively weighted active constraint has zero directional change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ay\leq b\}\) be nonempty, let \(x\in C\), and set \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^\mathsf{T}x=b_i\}\). Then \[T_C(x)=\{d:a_i^\mathsf{T}d\leq0\text{ for all }i\in I(x)\},\qquad N_C(x)=\{A_{I(x)}^\mathsf{T}\lambda:\lambda\geq0\}.\] If \(d\in T_C(x)\) and \(v=A_{I(x)}^\mathsf{T}\lambda\in N_C(x)\), then \[\langle v,d\rangle=\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i^\mathsf{T}d\leq0,\] and equality holds if and only if \(\lambda_i a_i^\mathsf{T}d=0\) for every \(i\in I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle v,d\rangle=0\) if and only if \(\lambda_i a_i^\mathsf{T}d=0\) for every \(i\in I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional polyhedral active-set form of tangent-normal complementarity.

notation.meaning: indices of inequalities active at x
row normal of the ith inequality

source_witnesses.locator: Sections 6.1 and 6.4, Convex Cones and Tangent and Normal Cones, pp. 111 and 125

children.top_down_role: Connection between polar local geometry and facial structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Faces of the Local Polar Pair
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal conjugation reverses inclusion and bijects the exposed faces of the tangent and normal cones. For a nonexposed face, double conjugation instead returns its smallest exposed hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:=T_C(x)\) and \(K^\circ=N_C(x)\). For a nonempty face \(F\unlhd K\), define \(F^\triangle:=K^\circ\cap F^\perp\), and define conjugation symmetrically for faces of \(K^\circ\). Then \(F^\triangle\) is an exposed face of \(K^\circ\), and \(F^{\triangle\triangle}\) is the smallest exposed face of \(K\) containing \(F\). Consequently, \(F^{\triangle\triangle}=F\) exactly when \(F\) is exposed, and conjugation restricts to an inclusion-reversing bijection between the exposed faces of \(K\) and those of \(K^\circ\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(x\in C\).
\(K=T_C(x)\) and \(K^\circ=N_C(x)\) use the nonpositive polar convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^{\triangle\triangle}=F\ \Longleftrightarrow\ F\text{ is exposed},\quad\text{and }F\mapsto F^\triangle\text{ bijects the exposed faces of }T_C(x)\text{ and }N_C(x)\text{ in reverse order}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-reversing correspondence for exposed faces of the mutually polar tangent and normal cones, including its exact nonexposed-face boundary.

notation.meaning: Conjugate face in the polar cone
Orthogonal complement of the linear span of the face

knowledge_statements.title: Facial Interpretation of Local Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero normal vector exposes the face of the tangent cone consisting of feasible first-order directions orthogonal to that vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_C(x):=\operatorname{cl}\{t(z-x):t\ge 0,\ z\in C\}\). Polarity gives \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\). For every \(y\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\), the set \[F_y=\{d\in T_C(x):\langle y,d\rangle=0\}=T_C(x)\cap y^\perp\] is an exposed face of the tangent cone on which the polar inequality \(\langle y,d\rangle\le 0\) is active. Thus a nonzero normal direction identifies precisely the tangent directions complementary to that normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_y:=T_C(x)\cap y^\perp\) is an exposed face of \(T_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional facial interpretation of a nonzero normal exposing directions in the tangent cone.

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone of the convex set at the reference point
orthogonal hyperplane to the nonzero normal vector

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, \(x\in C\), and \(s\in N_C(x)\). Define the exposed face \(F_C(s):=\{y\in C:\langle s,y\rangle=\langle s,x\rangle\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exposed facial geometry localized at a point belonging to the exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial interpretation of local polarity associates with \(s\in N_C(x)\) the directions on which the polar inequality is active. These directions are simultaneously the tangent cone to the exposed face and the orthogonal face of the tangent cone: \[T_{F_C(s)}(x)=T_C(x)\cap s^\perp=\{d\in T_C(x):\langle s,d\rangle=0\}.\] Thus strict negativity identifies directions entering below the supporting hyperplane, while equality identifies first-order motion within the face exposed by \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal exposes a face containing the base point. The tangent directions that remain in that exposed face are exactly the tangent directions orthogonal to the normal. Hence the zero set of the local polar pairing is the tangent geometry of the exposed face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{F_C(s)}(x)=T_C(x)\cap s^\perp.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in T_{F_C(s)}(x)\iff d\in T_C(x)\ \text{and}\ \langle s,d\rangle=0.\]
\[s\in N_C(x)\iff x\in F_C(s).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(s=0\), then \(F_C(0)=C\) and the identity is tautological.
For a polyhedron, choosing an active facet normal restricts the tangent cone by turning that active inequality into an equality.
immediate_consequences_latex: The complementary tangent directions form an exposed face of \(T_C(x)\).
Several active normals intersect their orthogonal tangent faces and thereby describe lower-dimensional local facial motion.
boundary_notes: Only exposed faces arise directly from a single normal vector.
The identity concerns first-order geometry at \(x\); it does not assert that nearby boundary points lie on a smooth manifold.

notation.meaning: face of C exposed by s
tangent cone to the exposed face at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asserted equality \(T_{F_C(s)}(x)=T_C(x)\cap s^\perp\) is false in general. For example, at a smooth exposed point of a Euclidean ball, the exposed face is a singleton and has tangent cone \(\{0\}\), while the right-hand side is the nonzero tangent hyperplane.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-reversing correspondence between exposed faces of the mutually polar tangent and normal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:=T_C(x)\) and \(K^\circ=N_C(x)\). For a face \(F\subseteq K\), define \(F^\triangle:=K^\circ\cap F^\perp\). If \(F\) is an exposed face of \(K\), then \(F^\triangle\) is an exposed face of \(K^\circ\), \((F^\triangle)^\triangle=F\), and \(F_1\subseteq F_2\) implies \(F_2^\triangle\subseteq F_1^\triangle\). The same construction starting from an exposed face of \(K^\circ\) gives the inverse correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal conjugation gives an inclusion-reversing bijection between exposed tangent-cone faces and exposed normal-cone faces.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(x\in C\).
\(T_C(x)\) and \(N_C(x)\) use the nonpositive polar convention, so \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operation \(F\mapsto N_C(x)\cap F^\perp\) is an inclusion-reversing bijection between the exposed faces of \(T_C(x)\) and those of \(N_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: Conjugate face of an exposed tangent-cone face
Orthogonal complement of the linear span of the face

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calculus of tangent and normal cone fields
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let all sets below be nonempty, closed, and convex in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and let every base point belong to the indicated set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact product and Minkowski-sum rules together with unconditional intersection inclusions; closure is retained where linear images or cone sums need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Local cone calculus is the collection of operation rules transporting tangent-normal pairs through convex-set constructions. In particular, \[T_{C_1\times C_2}(x_1,x_2)=T_{C_1}(x_1)\times T_{C_2}(x_2),\quad N_{C_1\times C_2}(x_1,x_2)=N_{C_1}(x_1)\times N_{C_2}(x_2),\] and \[T_{C_1+C_2}(x_1+x_2)=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(T_{C_1}(x_1)+T_{C_2}(x_2)\bigr),\quad N_{C_1+C_2}(x_1+x_2)=N_{C_1}(x_1)\cap N_{C_2}(x_2).\] For intersections, the unconditional relations are \[T_{C_1\cap C_2}(x)\subseteq T_{C_1}(x)\cap T_{C_2}(x),\quad N_{C_1\cap C_2}(x)\supseteq N_{C_1}(x)+N_{C_2}(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local cone calculus transports tangent and normal cones through products, sums, intersections, and affine operations. Products and Minkowski sums have the displayed exact rules, while intersections give inclusions unless a qualification condition is added.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in C_i\), and \(x\in C_1\cap C_2\) for the intersection rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tangent-normal assignments obey the displayed product, Minkowski-sum, and intersection rules.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The normal formulas are polar counterparts of the tangent formulas under \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: Cartesian powers satisfy \(T_{C^m}(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\prod_iT_C(x_i)\).
Translation does not change cone shape: \(T_{C+b}(x+b)=T_C(x)\) and \(N_{C+b}(x+b)=N_C(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite products and sums follow by iteration.
Qualification conditions are needed specifically where an unconditional inclusion may be strict.
boundary_notes: Closure in a tangent image or sum cannot be discarded without an additional closedness condition.
The rules are stated for convex sets; nonconvex tangent-normal calculi require different qualifications.

children.title: Local Cones of Intersections
children.top_down_role: Local geometry of aggregated convex constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Intersection Rule for Radial Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many convex constraints, the radial or feasible-direction cone of their intersection is exactly the intersection of their radial cones, without a constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite family of convex sets with \(x\in C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\), let \(R_D(x)=\operatorname{cone}(D-x)\). Then \[R_C(x)=\bigcap_{i=1}^mR_{C_i}(x).\] Equivalently, a direction admits a sufficiently small feasible step for the intersection exactly when it admits one for every constituent set.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\), with \(m\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_C(x)=\bigcap_{i=1}^mR_{C_i}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness permits one common positive step. Unlike equality for closed tangent cones, this radial-cone identity requires no relative-interior qualification.

notation.meaning: radial cone of D at x
finite intersection of the constraint sets

knowledge_statements.title: Local Cones of Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a common relative-interior point, the tangent cone of an intersection is the intersection of tangent cones, and its normal cone is their sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\), one always has \(T_C(x)\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(x)\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x)\subseteq N_C(x)\). Under the relative-interior qualification \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing\), both inclusions become equalities: \[T_C(x)=\bigcap_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(x),\qquad N_C(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x).\] Hence feasible first-order directions intersect, while constraint normals add.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty closed convex sets and \(x\in C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(x)=\bigcap_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(x)\) and \(N_C(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections under the standard relative-interior qualification.

notation.meaning: tangent cone at the common feasible point
normal cone at the common feasible point

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets, let \(C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\), and fix \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections in finite-dimensional convex analysis; exactness is separated from the unconditional inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local cones of an intersection obey \[T_C(x)\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(x),\qquad N_C(x)\supseteq\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x).\] If the relative-interior qualification \[\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing\] holds, these become the exact calculus formulas \[T_C(x)=\bigcap_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(x),\qquad N_C(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any tangent direction to an intersection must be tangent to every constituent set, and constituent normals add to normals of the intersection. Under a common relative-interior qualification, both inclusions become equalities.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty, closed, and convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{\cap_iC_i}(x)=\cap_iT_{C_i}(x),\qquad N_{\cap_iC_i}(x)=\sum_iN_{C_i}(x)\] under the stated relative-interior qualification.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For two sets, the qualification can be written \[0\in\operatorname{ri}(C_1-C_2)\iff \operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2\ne\varnothing.\]
special_cases_latex: For polyhedral sets, the normal sum collects the active constraint normals from all constituent systems.
If one set is the whole space, its tangent cone is \(\mathbb R^n\) and its normal cone is \(\{0\}\), leaving the other local cones unchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under qualification, tangent feasibility can be checked constituentwise.
Under qualification, every intersection normal decomposes as a sum \(s=\sum_i s_i\) with \(s_i\in N_{C_i}(x)\).
boundary_notes: Without qualification, the tangent inclusion and normal inclusion can be strict.
The common relative-interior condition is sufficient; more specialized transversality conditions may also yield exactness.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the constituent normal cones

knowledge_statements.title: Local Cones of an Affine Image
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangents to an affine image are the closure of the mapped tangent cone, and image normals are exactly those vectors whose transpose pullbacks are source normals. For an affine isomorphism, both transformations are exact without closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D:=A(C)+b\), choose \(x\in C\), and set \(y:=Ax+b\). Then \[T_D(y)=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(A(T_C(x))\bigr),\qquad N_D(y)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^m:A^\top v\in N_C(x)\}.\] These expressions are independent of the chosen \(x\) in the fiber \(C\cap A^{-1}(y-b)\). If \(A\) is a linear isomorphism, the closure is unnecessary and \(N_D(y)=A^{-\top}N_C(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear, and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_D(y)=\operatorname{cl}(A(T_C(x)))\quad\text{and}\quad N_D(y)=(A^\top)^{-1}(N_C(x)).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-image transport formulas, including the closure required for mapped tangent cones and the isomorphism specialization.

notation.meaning: Affine image of the source set
Set-theoretic inverse image of the normal cone under the transpose
Inverse transpose when the linear map is an isomorphism

knowledge_statements.title: Local Cones Under Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the affine range meeting the target's relative interior, tangents lift by inverse image and normals pull back by the transpose.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the affine inverse image \(Q=\{x:Ax+b\in C\}\), the qualified tangent and normal formulas at \(x\in Q\), with \(z=Ax+b\), are \[T_Q(x)=A^{-1}(T_C(z))=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\in T_C(z)\},\qquad N_Q(x)=A^\top N_C(z).\] Thus tangent directions lift through the linear part of the affine map, whereas target normals pull back through its transpose.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear; and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_Q(x)=\{d:Ad\in T_C(z)\}\) and \(N_Q(x)=A^\top N_C(z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine inverse-image calculus under a relative-interior range qualification.

notation.meaning: affine inverse image of the target set

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(A(z)=b+A_0z\) with linear part \(A_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and let \(x\in C\), \(y=A(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional direct affine images; closures and adjoint preimages are retained to cover noninjective and non-surjective maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local tangent cone transported from \(C\) through \(A\) is \[T_{A(C)}(y)=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(A_0T_C(x)\bigr).\] The normal cone transforms contravariantly: \[N_{A(C)}(y)=\{v\in\mathbb R^m:A_0^*v\in N_C(x)\},\] whenever \(x\) represents the local fiber at \(y\); in general the right-hand condition must hold for every \(z\in C\) with \(A(z)=y\). Thus tangent directions are pushed forward by \(A_0\), while normals are pulled back by its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under an affine map, tangent directions are sent forward by the linear part and then closed. A vector normal to the image is characterized by its adjoint pullback being normal to the original set at every point in the relevant fiber.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
For the single-point normal formula, the fiber \(C\cap A^{-1}(A(x))\) has the same normal pullback condition as at \(x\), in particular when \(A_0\) is injective on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{A(C)}(A(x))=\operatorname{cl}(A_0T_C(x)),\qquad N_{A(C)}(A(x))=\{v:A_0^*v\in N_C(x)\}\] in the stated single-fiber regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For arbitrary fibers, \[N_{A(C)}(y)=\{v:A_0^*v\in\bigcap_{z\in C,\ A(z)=y}N_C(z)\}.\]
For a translation \(A_0=I\), \[T_{C+b}(x+b)=T_C(x),\qquad N_{C+b}(x+b)=N_C(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(A_0\) is an orthogonal isomorphism, the closure is unnecessary and both cones are rotated by \(A_0\).
If \(C=C_1\times C_2\) and \(A_0(x_1,x_2)=x_1+x_2\), the tangent formula yields the Minkowski-sum rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: Affine translations affect the base point but not the cone shape.
Loss of directions under a rank-deficient map is reflected dually by the adjoint condition on normals.
boundary_notes: A linear image of a closed convex cone need not be closed, which explains the closure in the tangent formula.
For a nontrivial fiber, using the normal cone at only one arbitrary preimage can overstate the image normal cone.

children.title: Qualification Boundaries for Local Cone Calculus
children.top_down_role: Degenerate configurations in which expected local calculus relations fail.

knowledge_statements.title: Unqualified One-Sided Local Cone Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without qualification, intersection calculus retains only one-sided tangent and normal-cone inclusions; both can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\geq1\), let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, set \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\), and let \(x\in C\). Then
\[
T_C(x)\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(x),\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x)\subseteq N_C(x).
\]
Either inclusion can be strict when the relative-interior qualification fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_C(x)\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(x)\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x)\subseteq N_C(x).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These inclusions are unconditional; a qualification is needed to promote them to equalities.

notation.meaning: closed tangent cone of C at x
convex normal cone of C at x

knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Boundaries for Local Cone Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two tangent parabolic constraints intersect only at the origin, but their tangent halfspaces share a line; the corresponding normal-sum formula also fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Here \(C=C_1\cap C_2=\{x\}\), so \(T_C(x)=\{0\}\) and \(N_C(x)=\mathbb{R}^2\). However, \[T_{C_1}(x)=\{(p,q):q\ge0\},\qquad T_{C_2}(x)=\{(p,q):q\le0\},\] whence \(T_{C_1}(x)\cap T_{C_2}(x)=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\). Moreover, both individual normal cones are vertical rays, so their sum is \(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\), strictly smaller than \(N_C(x)\). The missing relative-interior qualification therefore destroys both expected equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(x)\subsetneq T_{C_1}(x)\cap T_{C_2}(x)\) and \(N_{C_1}(x)+N_{C_2}(x)\subsetneq N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of intersection calculus when relative interiors do not meet.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualification and Degeneracy of Linearized Local Cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\), where each \(c_j\) is convex, and let \(\bar x\in C\). Write \(J(\bar x)=\{j:c_j(\bar x)=0\}\), let \(T_C(\bar x)\) and \(N_C(\bar x)\) be the tangent and normal cones, and define the constraint-linearized cones \(T'(\bar x)\) and \(N'(\bar x)\) below.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex constraint systems; the definition distinguishes exact local cone calculus from representation-dependent degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linearized tangent cone and generated normal cone at \(\bar x\) are
\[T'(\bar x):=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:Ad=0,\ c_j'(\bar x;d)\leq0\ \forall j\in J(\bar x)\},\]
\[N'(\bar x):=\left\{A^\top\lambda+\sum_{j\in J(\bar x)}\mu_js_j:\lambda\in\mathbb R^m,\ \mu_j\geq0,\ s_j\in\partial c_j(\bar x)\right\}.\]
The representation is qualified for local cone calculus at \(\bar x\) when
\[T_C(\bar x)=T'(\bar x)\quad\text{and}\quad N_C(\bar x)=N'(\bar x).\]
Its qualification boundary consists of feasible points where at least one equality fails. A primal degeneracy is \(T_C(\bar x)\subsetneq T'(\bar x)\); a dual degeneracy is \(N'(\bar x)\subsetneq N_C(\bar x)\), including the case in which \(N'(\bar x)\) is nonclosed and only \(\operatorname{cl}N'(\bar x)\) agrees with \(N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set represented by affine equalities and convex inequalities, the constraint data define a linearized tangent cone from the active directional inequalities and a generated normal cone from equality normals and nonnegative combinations of active subgradients. Local cone calculus is qualified at a feasible point precisely when these data-derived cones equal the intrinsic tangent and normal cones. The qualification boundary is the set of feasible points where either equality fails. Thus degeneracy is representation-dependent: the same feasible set can have exact cone formulas under one constraint representation and strict inclusions under another.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in C\) and every \(c_j\) is convex and directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\).
The tangent and normal cones use the Euclidean finite-dimensional convention, with \(N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x\text{ is a qualification-boundary point}\iff T_C(\bar x)\neq T'(\bar x)\ \text{or}\ N_C(\bar x)\neq N'(\bar x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The basic constraint qualification at \(\bar x\) is the dual equality \(N'(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\); it entails closedness of \(N'(\bar x)\) and the corresponding tangent equality.
Failure can be detected by a direction in \(T'(\bar x)\setminus T_C(\bar x)\) or a normal in \(N_C(\bar x)\setminus N'(\bar x)\).
special_cases_latex: For affine equalities and affine inequalities, \(N_C(\bar x)=\operatorname{Im}A^\top+\operatorname{cone}\{s_j:j\in J(\bar x)\}\), so the basic qualification holds at every feasible point.
Representing \(C\) by \(\tfrac12d_C(x)^2\leq0\) gives a zero generated normal at boundary points and can therefore create degeneracy.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a qualified point, intrinsic first-order conditions may be written entirely using active constraint data.
At an unqualified point, replacing \(T_C\) by \(T'\) or \(N_C\) by \(N'\) can lose necessary local information.
boundary_notes: The definition concerns exact first-order cone calculus, not metric regularity or second-order constraint qualifications.
Equality with \(\operatorname{cl}N'(\bar x)\) alone does not remove the multiplier-attainment failure caused by a nonclosed \(N'(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Active inequality index set at the feasible point.
Constraint-linearized tangent cone and constraint-generated normal cone.

children.title: Hyperplane Separation and Support
children.top_down_role: Hyperplane separation, boundary support, outer representation, and failure boundaries.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb R^n\). For \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), set \(H(a,\beta)=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=\beta\}\), with closed half-spaces \(H^-(a,\beta)\) and \(H^+(a,\beta)\) defined by \(\leq\beta\) and \(\geq\beta\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine-hyperplane geometry for arbitrary nonempty sets, with convexity imposed when separation and support existence results are invoked.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An affine hyperplane \(H(a,\beta)\) separates nonempty sets \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) when
\[A\subseteq H^-(a,\beta),\qquad B\subseteq H^+(a,\beta),\]
equivalently
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta\leq\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
It strictly separates them when both displayed half-space inclusions use open half-spaces, equivalently
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle<\beta<\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
The hyperplane supports a nonempty set \(C\) when \(C\) lies in one closed half-space and meets the hyperplane; in the chosen orientation,
\[C\subseteq H^-(a,\beta),\qquad C\cap H(a,\beta)\neq\varnothing.\]
The contact set \(C\cap H(a,\beta)\) is the exposed face selected by \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero normal and scalar define an affine hyperplane and its two half-spaces. The hyperplane separates two sets when they lie in opposite closed half-spaces and strictly separates them when they lie in opposite open half-spaces. It supports a set when the entire set lies on one closed side and at least one point of the set lies on the hyperplane. For a convex set, the contact set is an exposed face. Reversing the normal exchanges the two orientations without changing the underlying hyperplane.
assumptions_latex: \(a\neq0\) so that \(H(a,\beta)\) is an affine hyperplane.
All suprema and infima are interpreted in the extended-real sense unless finiteness is explicitly required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[H(a,\beta)\text{ supports }C\iff \beta=\sigma_C(a)<+\infty\ \text{and}\ \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Separation is equivalently \(\sigma_A(a)+\sigma_B(-a)\leq0\) after translating the separating level to zero.
Support at \(x\in C\) is equivalently \(a\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta=\langle a,x\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For a cone, a supporting hyperplane at the origin is homogeneous: \(\beta=0\).
For a singleton \(B=\{z\}\), strict separation reduces to \(\sigma_A(a)<\langle a,z\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every supporting hyperplane that meets a convex set determines an exposed face.
A closed convex set equals the intersection of all closed half-spaces containing it.
boundary_notes: A half-space containing \(C\) need not support \(C\) if its boundary does not meet \(C\).

A hyperplane containing all of a lower-dimensional set is a trivial ambient support; nontrivial relative support requires a normal with nonzero component in the direction space of \(\operatorname{aff}C\).

notation.meaning: The two closed half-spaces bounded by \(H(a,\beta)\).

children.title: Separation Problem Geometries
children.top_down_role: Canonical configurations to which separation principles apply.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and let \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). A separation problem asks for a nonzero linear functional whose values order two prescribed geometric objects.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A classification of finite-dimensional convex separation problems by the objects being separated and by whether the separating hyperplane is affine or homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A separation problem geometry is one of the following configurations:
\[(\mathrm{PS})\quad z\notin C,\qquad \{z\}\ \text{versus a convex set }C;\]
\[(\mathrm{SS})\quad A\cap B=\varnothing,\qquad A\ \text{versus }B;\]
\[(\mathrm{H})\quad 0\notin D,\qquad \{0\}\ \text{versus a convex set }D,\]
where the homogeneous case requires a separator through the origin. In every case, a certificate is a pair \((a,\beta)\), \(a\neq0\), satisfying
\[\sup_{x\in A_0}\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta\leq\inf_{y\in B_0}\langle a,y\rangle,\]
with \((A_0,B_0)=(C,\{z\})\), \((A,B)\), or an oriented version of \((D,\{0\})\). Strict separation replaces the weak ordering by a positive gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical separation problems have three geometries. Point-set separation compares an exterior point with a convex set. Set-set separation compares two disjoint convex sets. Homogeneous separation compares the origin with a convex set or cone and seeks a hyperplane through the origin. In each geometry, a certificate is a nonzero linear functional and a level that place the two objects in opposite closed half-spaces; a strict certificate leaves a positive interval between their functional values.
assumptions_latex: The sets named in each configuration are nonempty and convex.
The disjointness or exterior-point condition is part of the problem data, not part of the certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{A valid separation certificate orders the two image intervals under }x\mapsto\langle a,x\rangle.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Set-set separation is point-set separation of \(0\) from the difference set \(A-B\).
Point-set separation is set-set separation with one set equal to a singleton.
A separator is homogeneous exactly when its level can be chosen as \(\beta=0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed convex and \(z\notin C\), the point-set geometry admits a strict certificate.
If one of two disjoint closed convex sets is bounded, the set-set geometry admits a positive-gap certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: Translation by the same vector preserves separation geometry and functional gaps.
Difference-set reformulation converts many set-set questions into origin-exclusion questions.
boundary_notes: Disjointness alone does not guarantee strict separation for two unbounded convex sets.
Weak separation can be geometrically trivial in the full ambient space when both sets lie in a proper affine subspace.

notation.meaning: Point-set, set-set, and homogeneous separation configurations.

children.title: Point-Set Separation
children.top_down_role: Separation of an exterior point from a convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Point-Set Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point outside a nonempty closed convex set can be strictly separated from it by an affine hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist a nonzero vector \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and a scalar \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \[\langle a,x\rangle<\alpha\le\inf_{c\in C}\langle a,c\rangle.\] Equivalently, an affine hyperplane strictly separates the exterior point from the closed convex set. If \(p=P_Cx\) is the Euclidean projection, one may take \(a=p-x\); then \(\langle a,c-p\rangle\ge0\) for all \(c\in C\), yielding a positive separating margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(a\ne0\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle<\alpha\le\langle a,c\rangle\) for every \(c\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong finite-dimensional separation of an exterior point from a closed convex set.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(z\in\mathbb R^n\setminus C\). For \(a\neq0\), compare \(\langle a,z\rangle\) with the support value \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional separation of one exterior point from a convex target; closedness is not built into the definition but controls the existence of a strict certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(z\) and set \(C\) are weakly separated when there exist \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta\leq\langle a,z\rangle\qquad\forall x\in C.\]
They are strongly separated when
\[\sigma_C(a)<\langle a,z\rangle,\]
equivalently when some \(\beta\) satisfies
\[\langle a,x\rangle<\beta<\langle a,z\rangle\qquad\forall x\in C.\]
The normalized directional margin of the certificate is
\[m(a;z,C):=\frac{\langle a,z\rangle-\sigma_C(a)}{\|a\|}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exterior point and a set are weakly separated if a nonzero linear functional places the set at or below a level and the point at or above it. They are strongly separated if the point's functional value is strictly greater than the support value of the set. Dividing this positive gap by the norm of the functional gives a scale-invariant directional margin. Reversing the functional yields the equivalent opposite orientation.
assumptions_latex: For a finite strong margin, the chosen direction satisfies \(\sigma_C(a)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[z\text{ is strongly separable from }C\text{ by }a\iff m(a;z,C)>0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strong separation is \(\langle a,z\rangle>\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\).
After translation, it is homogeneous strict separation of \(0\) from \(C-z\).
For closed convex \(C\), membership has the support-function characterization \(z\in C\iff\langle a,z\rangle\leq\sigma_C(a)\) for every \(a\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed convex, every \(z\notin C\) is strongly separable from \(C\).
If \(p=P_Cz\), then \(a=z-p\) is a separating direction and the normalized gap equals \(\|z-p\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strong certificate proves \(z\notin\operatorname{cl}C\).
Any positive rescaling of \(a\) preserves the normalized margin.
boundary_notes: If \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), no positive-gap separator exists, although weak separation may exist.
Point-set separation does not require the separating hyperplane to support \(C\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection of \(z\) onto a nonempty closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Set Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two nonempty disjoint convex sets in finite dimensions admit a separating hyperplane, although the separating margin may be zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[\langle a,c\rangle\le\alpha\le\langle a,d\rangle\qquad\text{for every }c\in C\text{ and }d\in D.\] Equivalently, \(\sup_{c\in C}\langle a,c\rangle\le\inf_{d\in D}\langle a,d\rangle\). No positive gap is asserted; additional closedness, compactness, or distance assumptions are needed for strong separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(a\ne0\) such that \(\sup_{c\in C}\langle a,c\rangle\le\inf_{d\in D}\langle a,d\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak finite-dimensional separation of two arbitrary disjoint convex sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak, Proper, and Strict Set Separation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets. Orient a prospective separator so that functional values on \(A\) do not exceed those on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex set-set separation, explicitly distinguishing weak, proper, and positive-gap notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(A\) and \(B\) are weakly separated by \(a\neq0\) if
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle\leq\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
They are properly separated by \(a\) if this inequality holds and the functional is not constant across both sets, namely
\[\inf_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle<\sup_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
They are strictly, or strongly, separated by \(a\) if
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle<\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
In the strict case, every level strictly between the two bounds defines an affine hyperplane placing \(A\) and \(B\) in opposite open half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty convex sets are weakly separated when a nonzero linear functional orders all points of the first set below all points of the second. Separation is proper when this ordering is not merely caused by the functional being constant on their common affine environment. It is strict or strong when there is a positive gap between the largest value on the first set and the smallest value on the second. Any scalar inside that gap is the level of a strictly separating hyperplane.
assumptions_latex: The orientation is conventional and may be reversed by replacing \(a\) with \(-a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A,B\text{ are strictly separated by }a\iff \sigma_A(a)+\sigma_B(-a)<0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Weak separation is \(\sigma_A(a)+\sigma_B(-a)\leq0\).
Strict separation is strict point-set separation of \(0\) from \(A-B\).
Proper separation excludes the case in which \(\langle a,\cdot\rangle\) has one common value on \(A\cup B\).
special_cases_latex: When \(B=\{z\}\), strict set-set separation is strict point-set separation.
If \(A,B\) are closed and disjoint and one is bounded, they are strictly separable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict separation implies \(A\cap B=\varnothing\).
Proper separation is available when \(\operatorname{ri}A\cap\operatorname{ri}B=\varnothing\).
boundary_notes: Weak separation alone may be improper for lower-dimensional sets.
Disjoint closed unbounded convex sets need not possess a positive-gap separator.

notation.meaning: Support-function expression for the oriented functional gap.
